Tuning is on seeds 1-8, held-out 31-60, and the confirmation uses the same frozen tuning on 61-90. Tests are paired 95% t-CI with Holm per family, over 7-10 worlds plus controls in each part.

Everything is measured in my own synthetic world, so none of it says anything about real LLM traffic. No claims of novel knowledge, emergence or "10x".

**(a) Retrieval before routing**
- **Neighbour retrieval is already good once the store is dense.** The `research.rs` default (raw cosine, threshold .6, k5) gets F1 .989 at low noise, .933 for paraphrase, and .594 in a sparse 96-concept world.
- **The tuned configs beat the default in all 9 treatment worlds on both seed sets (Holm).** The gain is +.003 to +.068 F1, and most of it comes from k3 vs k5 rather than centering.
- **Mean-centering matters only in sparse many-concept worlds.** There it adds +.006 (48 concepts) and +.014 (96 concepts) F1 over tuned raw. In dense worlds it is neutral, and it loses early (first 300 queries: -.013 to -.032 at noise 1.2-1.6; Holm LOSS at noise 1.6 on both seed sets).
- **Query expansion helps less than the retune (+.001 to +.023), relative-margin does nothing, and MMR diversity hurts.** MMR is a Holm LOSS in 9 of 9 worlds for raw cosine and 4 of 9 for centered.
- **No single threshold serves both the neighbour list and the anchor vote.** Anchor pair-F1 is only .40 at low noise and .08-.17 in the many-concept worlds. A threshold tuned for the anchors raises it by +.45 but costs -.09 to -.30 neighbour F1.
- **Downstream, the best retriever adds +.027 to +.060 gross quality over warm+reuse without retrieval (Holm WIN).** It adds only +.004 (n.s.) over the default in the main world, and +.017/+.022 in the 48-concept world.
- **Oracle retrieval would add another +.003 (n.s.) at low noise and +.026 to +.032 in the hard worlds.**

**(b) Sample efficiency (graded outcomes until the trailing quality or accuracy target is reached)**
- **Reuse path:** about 330-560 fewer outcomes to quality ≥ .80, Holm WIN in every treatment world on both seed sets. Gross quality gains +.075 to +.129, and it also helps in the irrelevant-notes world, so it is the known reuse effect and not retrieval.
- **Warm start:** gross +.027 to +.047 on 31-60 (WIN in the 5 treatment worlds). On 61-90 it is WIN in 3 of 5 treatment worlds and n.s. in the other two (+.020 to +.024). It is worth 198-355 fewer outcomes in the 48-concept world and in the main world on 61-90 (n.s. on 31-60).
- **Retrieval on top:** 92-164 fewer outcomes. Example in the main world: 196 outcomes with warm+reuse, 89 with the best retriever, 75 with the oracle.
- **Early horizon:** at 250 tasks warm+reuse (.744) is not better than the keyword router (.738), and the cold-start variant is much worse (.620).
- **Censoring:** plain and keyword routing often never reach the target, so the savings are lower bounds.
- **Controls:** the equal-agents world ties on every arm, and the irrelevant-notes world shows no harm or gain from retrieval.

**(c) Generator → critic (31 cells, cost per extra call .01/.03/.10)**
- **The e3 gate does not pay.** At cost .03 it is a Holm net LOSS in 24 of 31 cells on 31-60 (25 on 61-90) and never a WIN. It wins only in a few high-error cells at cost .01.
- **A calibrated trigger pays only in a narrow region.** Checking only when the generator's own confidence is below .3 wins when three things hold: confidence separates bad from good drafts (AUROC ≥ ~.9), at least ~15% of drafts are bad, and a check costs ≤ ~.03.
  - Gains in that region are about +.006 to +.023 net.
  - Example: with 30% base error and AUROC .93, +.0155 on 31-60 and +.0127 on 61-90, both Holm WIN.
  - At AUROC .7-.8, and at cost .10, it never pays. An uninformative confidence is net negative.
- **Retrieval-based triggers (no support, disagreement) do not work.** They catch only 3-15% of bad drafts.
- **Ceiling:** even a trigger that checks exactly the bad drafts gains only about +.03 to +.05, because the checker misses most of them and the retry errs again.
- **Control:** with no errors, every real critic is a small Holm LOSS.

**Caveats and disclosure (full list in the board block)**
- The embeddings, error and note-benefit models, and the self-confidence signal are mine. Real self-confidence AUROC is unknown, so read (c) along the AUROC grid.
- The critic uses the harsh replace-by-retry convention. A verifiable or best-of-two checker was not run and would favour the critic.
- I inspected a first 31-60 run before three fixes: a sign bug in the lower-is-better verdict, an "anchor purity" metric gamed by fragmentation (replaced by pair-F1), and a wider critic grid (new confidence levels, thresholds .1/.2). None of them changed the frozen retrieval choices or the part (b) tables.
- A 61-90 run on an older build was killed unread. The reported 61-90 numbers come from the final build, run once.

- **MiniLM with system work vs BGE alone, retrieval:** a statistical tie, not a robust win. MiniLM-final (spell-correct plus overlap rerank) vs BGE-alone: MRR +0.003 | +0.004 (not significant after Holm); hit@1 +0.011 (Holm win) | +0.005 (not significant).

- **MiniLM + hybrid vs BGE alone, routing (sib16, H2000):** +0.025 (Holm win) | +0.014 (not significant after Holm). This points toward system work beating a bigger model, but is small and not replicated at Holm level.
- **Per-lever effects:**
  - Spell-correct gives nearly all the gain, concentrated in the typo class (hit@1 .77 to .94).
  - Hybrid and rerank add about +0.01, raising top-1 but lowering recall@3 (R@3 .77 to .64 for MiniLM).
  - Chunk max-pool is neutral on MiniLM and -0.013 MRR on BGE.
  - Rocchio PRF is always negative or neutral.
  - Overlap rerank hurts chatty queries.
- **Cascade:** the MiniLM-to-BGE cascade is the best retrieval system (hit@1 .953), but it needs both encoders, so it costs more than BGE alone.
- **Controls:** the knowledge layer loses on the no-information control for every embedder, including the oracle (about -0.02 to -0.03). It is also slightly negative on mixed50, and weak at 64 concepts.

**Verdict.**
1. BGE earns a small retrieval edge (+2 to 3 points hit@1) but does not improve routing outcome.
2. System work on MiniLM roughly ties BGE alone on retrieval at about 1/5 the encode latency; it is not a clean win. It points the same way on routing, but small and unreplicated.
3. Keep MiniLM as the default and add spell-correction. A hybrid dense + tf-idf similarity is worth trying if routing matters. Re-test on real text before changing anything.

**Caveats I flagged in the entry.**
- The corpus is synthetic and templated, with only 3 surface forms per detail, so lexical methods look unrealistically strong.
- The system gain depends on my choice of 25% typo queries; on clean queries the MiniLM system gain is about zero or negative.
- Retrieval CIs are over resampled query subsets of one pool; the A to B replication is the independent check, and it agrees on all signs.
- The routing policy is a replica of the crate's knowledge-router semantics (not the crate itself), and weak-feedback regime W was not run.
- Latencies are from Python onnxruntime on a shared box.

- Applying novelty to every domain costs −0.002 to −0.15 on correctness value, so the gate is essential. A hard-shortlist variant sharing one router across domains cost −0.009 on the correctness half of M1.
- The learned gate starts off, so about 17% of creative tasks run ungated. It was wrong on 10% of tasks in K3 with no measurable harm.
- **Robustness failure.** I reran the frozen arms on value functions that differ from the policies' internal novelty model:
  - V1 (weaker novelty, mean-distance): `nbucb`/declared still wins, `nbucb`/learned does not, and `nbreg` wins small.
  - V2 (novelty practically unattainable): every arm loses to the best fair baseline in all creative worlds, by −0.02 to −0.06, Holm-significant. The gate stays on because it only sees an observational slope.
  - V3 (mild mismatch): `nbreg` wins clearly, e.g. +0.059/+0.052/+0.028 on held-out C1–C3.
- **R1 "rigged" check.** It is not truly uninformative: repeats of the same agent show up in both the observed and hidden dimensions. The bonus gives nothing there, −0.004 to −0.009 against the arm's own base, so the small win over the best fair baseline in R1 comes from the learner.

**Process disclosure (also in the entry):**
- Held-out 31–60 was viewed once before the final run. A bug in my reference rows (the "own base" comparison for `nbucb`) was fixed, and the arms themselves did not change. Only confirm 61–90 is clean of that.
- `nbreg` was added after I saw V2 and has no tuned parameters. V3 is the only clean out-of-sample check for it; V2 is not.
- The value function and the policies' internal novelty model share structure by my design.
- Only the `Oracle` arm reads the world view. I confirmed that by grep.

**Recommendation:** not a default and not a merge candidate. A gated, per-domain novelty bonus is a defensible opt-in only where a human declares the domain creative and a matching output-embedding novelty measure exists. Do not enable learned gating blind. I made no claims about real creativity or real traffic.

The F3 fix works: real `neural-mesh serve --port` throughput on loopback is 2.8x to 14x higher, and replies are byte-identical to round-2 HEAD in all 14 equivalence scenarios. Board entry with the rerun commands is in `C:\Users\mariu\neural-mesh\results\g6_board_entry.md` (one "### VERIFY REQUEST — W6 — SERVE-PERF" block). I only touched `src/serve.rs` under `src/`; there are no `Cargo.toml`/`Cargo.lock` changes, no new crates, and no commits. Every test server uses `--port 0` and the harness asserts it reports a `127.0.0.1:` address.

**Changes in `src/serve.rs` (default behaviour, no reply byte changes)**
- **One write per reply.** Each reply is serialised once into a reused buffer and sent with a single write. The old `writeln!` on the raw `TcpStream` issued about 124 writes per reply.
- **Batched flush.** If the client has more complete request lines already queued, replies are held and sent together (at most 64 KiB). They always go out before the server blocks for input, at EOF, and on `shutdown`. A unit test confirms a lockstep client still gets one write per reply and a 30-request burst gets one write.
- **Parse outside the global lock.** JSON parse, command lookup and field validation now run before taking the `Mutex<Server>`. The per-request allowed-list `Vec` and the array join allocations are gone.
- **Over-long lines are discarded as they stream in.** Lines over 1 MiB are no longer buffered whole; the reply is the same "request line too long". A 200 MB line peaks under 6 MB heap in a unit test.
- **Opt-in, default off:** env `NEURAL_MESH_SERVE_STAT_MS=N` checks the state file at most every N ms instead of before every request. I did not make it default because it changes when an external CLI write is absorbed (never lost). It needs your decision.

- The script is 2,839 lines: valid operations, about 85 hand-written error forms, 1,800 fuzzed lines, and lines at the 1 MiB boundary, 3 MiB lines and invalid UTF-8. Roughly 60% of replies are errors.
- It runs 14 scenarios over stdio and TCP: lockstep, one burst, random chunking, byte-at-a-time, EOF mid-line, half-close, shutdown mid-stream, and CLI writes interleaved. Reply bytes, exit codes and final state-file bytes are compared.
- Base-versus-base controls are all deterministic, and a one-byte-changed self-test is detected.
- The rebuilt baseline also matches the original one I used for the numbers.
- In-process there are 6 new serve tests, including a verbatim copy of the old loop compared byte for byte under 1-, 7- and 4093-byte reads.
- Test results: `cargo test --release --lib` 228 passed, 0 failed; `cargo test --release --bin neural-mesh` 19 passed, 1 ignored (the allocation report).

**Decisions/s, medians of 5 reps, base to new (route + feedback per decision)**

| Config | Base | New | Paired ratio (median [min..max]) |
|---|---|---|---|
| TCP lockstep, 1 client | 683 | 5,375 | 7.9x [7.1..9.3] |
| TCP lockstep, 2 clients | 956 | 7,408 | 7.2x |
| TCP lockstep, 4 clients | 1,727 | 6,593 | 4.2x |
| TCP lockstep, 8 clients | 2,517 | 6,915 | 2.8x [2.3..2.95] |
| TCP pipelined 32+32 per write, 1 client | 682 | 9,491 | 13.8x [12.3..15.1] |
| TCP pipelined, 4 clients | 1,749 | 10,281 | 5.9x |
| TCP pipelined, 8 clients | 2,624 | 9,533 | 3.6x |
| stdio, default flush | 7,705 | 8,230 | 1.12x (paired [0.90..1.31]) — not significant |
| stdio, flush off | 11,292 | 15,304 | 1.24x |

- Server CPU per decision at lockstep with 1 client falls from 1,444 µs to 172 µs. Peak working set is unchanged at the default flush (7.5–8.3 MB).
- Allocations per request go from 66.0 to 62.4, about 5.5% fewer, so allocation was never the bottleneck. The remaining allocations sit in `cmd_route`/`cmd_feedback` in `main.rs` and the request `Value` tree, which `serve.rs` cannot change.
- The runs were ABAB-interleaved. A baseline-versus-copy-of-itself control gives a noise floor of roughly ±8% (paired ratios 0.72–1.24).
- Machine load caveat: system CPU was busy a median of 59% (33–97%) in the 250 ms before each run, so absolute numbers are depressed. Trust the paired ratios.

**Negatives**
- **Remaining server cost:** the per-request `fs::metadata` stat on the state file costs about 19 µs on this box. A cheaper Windows call (`GetFileAttributesExW`) only gets it to about 16 µs.
- **Opt-in knob results:** with `NEURAL_MESH_SERVE_STAT_MS=50`, stdio flush-off reaches about 88k decisions/s (5.6x over the default-new build), and TCP lockstep with 8 clients and flush off reaches 41k (4.2x). Those results are in `results/g6_bench_optin_stat50.json`.
- **Flush cost:** each count-triggered flush runs inside the global lock and costs an estimated 3–4 ms. Lockstep with 1 client does 5.4k decisions/s at the default flush versus 6.4k with flush off. Moving it off the request path means restructuring `commit()`, which I did not do.
- **Client scaling is still poor:** at the default flush, going from 1 to 8 clients only goes from 5.4k to 6.9k decisions/s.
- **Not tested:** Linux/macOS, more than 8 clients, the `internal error` panic reply (no input I tried reaches it), and byte equality across concurrent connections (arrival order makes it non-deterministic).

**1. Critic.** Worlds have four real error types (stale, wrong-entity, unsupported, arithmetic), run through the real `ResearchSession`. There are 14 worlds including zero-error controls, plus a report family of 4-claim answers. Tuning was on seeds 1-8, held-out 31-60, confirm 61-90, 30 seeds each. Net = accuracy − c·(extra agent calls + 0.1·evidence-tool runs), headline c = 0.05, shown as net@0.05; Holm WIN/LOSS counts are in the entry.
- **Shipped critic:** the research.rs gate, whose second agent does not see evidence, is effectively a no-op. It checks about 1% of tasks, catches 0.5% of errors, and its net is within ±0.001 of no critic in the A-family worlds. It is slightly negative in the 4-claim report worlds and the zero-error controls. This matches the earlier "critic off is right" finding.
- **Evidence-reading verifier:** per-source voting plus rerouting adds +0.054 to +0.071 net@0.05 in worlds A1-A6 (base retrieval). Errors drop from 0.103 to 0.007 unflagged in A1. Both splits agree, with a paired CI half-width of 0.004 or less.
- **Where it loses:** weak retrieval (A7, −0.008 to −0.012) and single-source poisoned evidence (A11, a world I added after seeing the first run, −0.03 to −0.04). It also loses in the zero-error controls (−0.007 to −0.014) and in the rare-error 4-claim world.
- **Online precision gate:** an `auto` variant gates acting on flags using the delayed graded outcomes. It matches the plain verifier above break-even and caps the losses below it at about −0.01.
- **Break-even surface:** the verifier pays when the current fact reaches the evidence at least about 0.5-0.65 of the time and the error rate is at least about 3-6%.
- **Self-consistency:** net-negative in every world at c ≥ 0.05, because it charges 2 extra calls on every task.

- **Why:** it is a lexical-lever effect, not a model effect. BGE with the same hybrid gains the same, and tf-idf alone beats BGE-alone in sib16 on corpus C.
- **Retrieval:** MiniLM with spell-correction plus overlap rerank now beats BGE-alone with Holm WINs on both corpora (hit@1 +0.012 and +0.023). W1 had called that a tie.
- **Tasks-to-target:** reaching 95% of the best baseline's level is uninformative; every system does it within about 130 tasks. Reaching half the headroom to the oracle takes 1000-1500 tasks for the retrieval systems. MiniLM+hybrid gets there 350-450 tasks sooner than BGE-alone in sib16 (Holm WIN on both corpora), and not elsewhere.
- **Control:** the knowledge layer still loses about 0.022 on irrelevant context for every similarity, including the oracle.

**3. Multi-step dependent sessions.** Sessions are 3-5 steps; step k+1's query is written from the retrieved evidence of step k. They run on real MiniLM and BGE vectors, with 5,760 machine-written follow-up queries per corpus. I report results for corpus C (seeds 31-60) and corpus D (seeds 61-90). Session success is the share of sessions with every step's top-1 correct.
- **Dependence:** it costs 7-9 step-accuracy points (e.g. MiniLM 0.895 vs 0.811). Session success is identical dependent vs independent by construction, so the penalty shows only in step accuracy and evidence recall.
- **Attribute-check verification:** checking the retrieved document's detail against the detail the query states lifts session success from 0.71-0.81 to 0.91-0.98 on all nine retrieval systems, even BM25. - **Hybrid caveat:** hybrid and rerank systems are higher on session success but lower on P@3/R@3.

**Blunt negatives**
- **Part 1 (evidence):** the critic is handed parsed, structured evidence, and I defined the error types in terms of that same evidence. The 0.9+ recall is a property of the construction.
- **Part 2 (corpora):** A, B, C and D come from one templated generator, so "replicated" means stable across corpus draws, not robust to real text.
- **Part 3 (verifier):** the gains are an upper bound. The verifier's gazetteer is the generator's own surface-form list, and it reads 478 of 480 documents correctly. If it knows only 1 of 3 forms the gain drops to about +0.03 to +0.07. With 10% wrong detections the `local` policy turns 0.78 into 0.64, while `pin` tolerates about 10-20%. There is no clean control world where verification should not help.

**Decisions for you**
- Should the evidence-aware verifier become a patch? The proposal is opt-in with the online gate, with `critic: None` staying the default. It is sketched in `g9_proposed_patch.md` (the other two sketches there are hybrid similarity with spell-correction, and constraint pinning).

- **Setup:** two independent families, 3 embedders each. F5 is the f5 corpus with hash, MiniLM and BGE. G1 is the hard sibling corpus, with corpus A for tuning and held-out seeds and corpus B as the fresh confirm corpus. Tuning on seeds 1-8, held 31-60, confirm 61-90, TOST margin ±0.01, Holm over all cells.
- **Specified rule** (running mean − k·std of top-1 cosine, one frozen kstd chosen on F5 and applied to G1 unchanged): 0 of 18 anchor-F1 cells were equivalent in held-out, and 0 of 18 in confirm. Mean paired diff was −0.14 on F5 and −0.05 on G1.
- **Vote routing success:** only 10 of 60 cells were equivalent in each split. Against the untuned library default (k5, sim .6), the rule is a tie.
- **Extra variant, labelled as such:** a chance-level floor (mean + 2·std of the cosine to random earlier queries). It recovers about 57% of the tuning gain on anchor F1 and about 44% on H2000, but is still 0 of 18 equivalent on anchor F1.
- **Why it fails:**
  - **Peaked F1:** F1 is sharply peaked in the threshold (MiniLM on F5: .907 at .50, .847 at .55).
  - **Tuned values do not map to a constant:** in top-1 sigmas the tuned values span kstd −1.6 to +2.3. In chance-level sigmas they span 1.4–2.45.
  - **Duplicates dominate:** 86–94% of top-1 hits in these worlds are exact duplicates.
- **Control caveat:** the unique-context control cannot show spurious anchors here, because the tuned incumbent also joins 97–99% of those tasks to an existing anchor. The routing cells on ctl-unique and ctl-irrel are the informative control.
- **Replay check:** the cached-neighbour replay I used matches the real `Knowledge` object, with 0 anchor mismatches in 36 runs.

- **Success:** no Holm win on H500 or H2000 in either family. Event(0.98) gives about +0.004–0.006 H2000 on the F5 drift-mid world, and 0 on G1. H500 is pre-drift and is about −0.008 for the discounted arms.

**What I built**
- New bin `src/bin/g11_team.rs` plus `src/bin/g11_common/{mod,world,base,learn}.rs`. No `src/*.rs` was touched, no new crates, no commits.
- **Worlds.** They do not share W7's generator: variable requirement-tag sets and noisy graded reward (noise sd 0.2). The primary metric is the noise-free team value `v`.
  - RC: coverage of weighted skill demands, with drift and large variants.
  - ROLE: 3 of 5 roles needed, plus a duplicate-role penalty.
  - THR: capability thresholds, near-additive.
  - LAT: additive plus pairwise by construction, so not independent evidence.
  - Two separable controls, C-SEP and C-SEPT; C-SEPT has a trap keyword map.
  - Set 1 (the eight worlds above) was frozen before any policy ran.
  - Set 2 is keyword-degraded copies of those worlds. I added it after the first dev run showed a perfect keyword table is close to the oracle in RC and ROLE.
  - Set 3 is COMP and COMP-X (hidden complementary pairs), added later.
- **Arms.** L-add (additive), L-pair (additive plus pairwise), L-gate (pair model used only when a prequential test favours it), and L-full (L-gate plus a causal controller gate between the learner and `seq:guarded-safe`).
- **Baselines.** Sequential routers with team credit, tuned per world on seeds 1-8, plus `NeuralMesh` with `team_size=K`. The best fair baseline is picked on the evaluation seeds, which is conservative.
- **Protocol.** Tuning on seeds 1-8 only, held 31-60, fresh confirm 61-90, and `--tune perworld` as the generous check. Paired 95% t-CI, Holm applied separately within each world set. Controls get TOST ±0.01 plus a one-sided non-inferiority test, and there is a reward-noise sensitivity run (`--noise 0.1` and `0.4`).

**Results for L-add** (difference in `v` vs the best fair baseline; held and confirm agree)

- **Set 2 (keyword table half wrong):** Holm wins in every world, and the sign is the same across held, confirm and per-world tuning.

  | World | Diff vs best fair |
  |---|---|
  | RC-K | about +0.065 |
  | RC-L-K | +0.08 |
  | ROLE-K | about +0.11 |
  | THR-K | +0.09 to +0.14 |

- **Set 1:**
  - THR +0.14 to +0.16, a win, but it is a near-additive world.
  - RC-drift +0.015 to +0.021, a win.
  - It loses to a perfect keyword table: RC −0.014, RC-L −0.007, ROLE −0.009 to −0.011. The per-world-tuned runs shrink these to −0.004 to −0.011, or n.s. for ROLE.
  - Against the repo default `seq:guarded-safe` the same worlds are RC −0.011, RC-L −0.002, ROLE +0.113.
- **Set 3:** COMP +0.09 to +0.10 and COMP-X +0.076, both wins. COMP-X was built to defeat a global pairwise term and did not hurt the additive model.

response:
W13 (G12) is done. The learned router loses to the best requested baseline in every existing world at every data volume I tested, up to 20000 tasks. It wins only in worlds I built with continuous features or XOR / RBF skill structure. Held (31-60) and confirm (61-90) results agree.

**Files** (`src/*.rs` untouched, no commits, no new crates)
- `src/bin/g12_annrouter.rs` and `src/bin/g12_common/mod.rs` (worlds, net, arm factory, driver, 6 unit tests).

- `results/g12_board_entry.md` (VERIFY REQUEST A-D blocks with rerun commands, tables, negatives) and `results/g12_proposed_patch.md` (proposes no patch).

**The router**
- A std-only f32 net: hashed token slots plus optional raw continuous features go into one tanh hidden layer, which outputs a logit per agent.
- It learns online by per-agent BCE regression on the same binary outcome the other arms see.
- Exploration is softmax with decaying temperature, plus an optional replay buffer. A policy-gradient mode was in the grid and never selected.
- Variants: `ann-tok` (no continuous features, for equal information), `ann+kw` (a keyword-prior skip connection), and a non-neural reference `pts-pairs` (pooled-thompson over pairwise token conjunctions).

**Worlds**
- Ten in total: sim Fixed/Random/NoTraps, f3 Big and BigTail (my copy takes T as a parameter and is unit-tested bit-identical to `f3_common` at T=4000), plus `lin-cont`, `xor-cont`, `xor-cont-drift`, `xor-tok` and `rich-cont`.
- The new worlds were fixed before any policy comparison, apart from one rescale of `rich-cont` (its oracle was only .40).

**Protocol**
- Knobs were tuned on seeds 1-8 per regime (T=2000 or 4000 for Big, 6000, 20000 using the 6000 config). The tuning is deterministic and gave identical configs in both runs.
- Each run used 30 seeds and a paired 95% CI against the best requested baseline, with Holm correction per regime. A claim needs Holm-WINs in at least 2 independent world families.

**Results** (full-stream mean success; the 61-90 confirm run agrees)
- **Existing worlds:** the net loses at every volume.
  - Sim gap vs the best baseline: about -.07 at 2000, -.04 at 6000, -.025 at 20000.
  - Big and BigTail gap: about -.19, -.17, -.13.
  - The gap narrows but never crosses. Even `ann+kw` still loses every sim/Big cell.
- **Continuous or interaction worlds:** the net wins, so that claim is kept. Counts are Holm WIN/LOSS per regime out of 10 worlds.
  - Held run, low/mid/high: 3W/6L, 5W/5L, 5W/5L. Confirm run: the same.
  - `xor-cont`: tie at 2000 (+.001), +.117 at 6000, +.177 at 20000.
  - `xor-tok`: about +.12 at 2000, +.24 at 20000.
  - `rich-cont`: +.026 at 2000, +.040 at 20000, so the margin grows with data.
- **Crossover** (tasks until the net is sustainedly at parity with the best baseline, from the 20000-task curves):

| world | tasks to parity |
|---|---|
| `lin-cont`, `rich-cont`, `xor-tok` | about 500 |
| `xor-cont` | about 1500 |
| `xor-cont-drift` | 11500 (dips below the baselines right after the T/2 swap) |
| sim, Big | never |

- **The hypothesis is only partly right.**
  - Confirmed: the net ties or loses in the existing keyword-token worlds.
  - Refuted: in worlds with continuous or interaction structure it is ahead within the first 500-1500 tasks, so nothing needs 6000+ tasks to flip.
  - The only "more data helps more" trend is `rich-cont`.
- **Cost** (single thread, shared box, about ±30% noise):
  - State: the selected H24 net with replay is about 120 kB and stays flat in T. `warm(hebr)` grows from 0.09 MB to 0.3 MB at 6 agents, and from 0.27 MB to 1.18 MB at 32 agents. `pts-pairs` reaches 7.9 MB.
  - ns/decision: about 2.2 µs on 6 agents and 4.2 µs on 32 agents. The 32-agent figure is below eps/pts/hebbian/warm/guarded (5.4-18.6 µs). An H8 net without replay costs about 0.6-1.2 µs.

**Caveats to carry forward**
- The win in `lin-cont` is an information advantage: the net sees raw floats and the baselines see 8-bin tokens. With equal information (`ann-tok`) the net loses at 2000 tasks and only ties by 20000.
- `pts-pairs` is as good as the net in token XOR at 6000+ tasks and better at 2000, though the 2000-task difference is not significant after Holm. The net's real edge over it is on the continuous worlds.
- The nonlinear worlds are nonlinear by my construction, so they show what the net can do, not that real task streams have such structure.
- Several tuned values sit at grid edges (the net's `half`=100, warm k=6, eps=0), so those arms might improve with wider grids.
- Capacity and hashing may limit the net in Big (H≤64, 256 slots, 3000-token tail vocabulary); I did not test a larger net.
- The board entry's `replay_entry_bytes` field undercounts at 80 B (actual about 92 B); the live-heap column is the measured figure.

`cargo run --release --offline --bin g12_annrouter -- --held 61-90 --out results/g12_annrouter_confirm61-90.json`

response:
W14 (TOOLS track) is done: tools, learned selection and caching are all built and measured, and the lift over the six plain baselines holds in both worlds. It is a simulation with assumed error rates. It does not show the frozen model getting smarter.

**Files** (nothing else touched; no Cargo or crate change, no git commit)
- `src/tools.rs` (new, std-only) plus the one line `pub mod tools;` appended to `src/lib.rs`.
- `src/bin/g13_tools.rs`, `src/bin/g13_common/mod.rs`.
- `results/g13_*` (`.json`/`.log` per mode), `results/g13_run_all.sh`, `results/g13_board_entry.md` (four "### VERIFY REQUEST — W14" blocks with rerun commands, numbers and negatives).

**What `tools.rs` contains**
- `Tool` trait and a `Registry` with a result cache and hit/saved-cost accounting.
- `Calc`: exact overflow-checked rationals with a precedence parser.
- `Units`: conversion plus dimension check.
- `Csp`: finite-domain solver and certificate checker.
- `Identity`: grid check for small symbolic claims.
- `Sandbox`: own tiny interpreter with step, memory, depth and size limits and no I/O.
- `LookupTool` for key/value tables.
- `Verifier`: re-computes a claim and returns accept or reject.
- `ToolSelector` for learned tool choice, and `tool_features()` for spec-shape tokens.

**Checks**
- `cargo test --release --offline --lib tools`: 21 passed, 0 failed. They cover parser edge cases, overflow, step limits, determinism, 25 sandbox escape attempts, wrong-tool inputs and cache correctness.
- `g13_tools selfcheck`: about 7,200 generated tasks. The real tools match natively computed truth on 100% of canonical specs. The verifier accepts 100% of correct outputs and rejects 100% of the wrong claims it was shown.
- The verifier reuses the same exact evaluator for calc, units and program tasks, so a systematic parser bug would not be caught by it.

**Headline results** (held seeds 31-60 and frozen confirm seeds 61-90, two independent world generators A and B, paired 95% CI, Holm over the 6 baselines)

| step | result vs best plain baseline | cost per task |
|---|---|---|
| S0: keyword picks the tool, plus verifier | +0.184 / +0.250 (held A/B), +0.186 / +0.235 (confirm A/B) | about 2x plain |
| S1: learned tool selection | +0.208 / +0.278 (held), +0.213 / +0.263 (confirm); every Holm p below 1e-23 | 18.6-19.8 vs 10.0 |

- S1 beats S0 in correctness by +0.024 to +0.028 and is cheaper than S0 by 1.7-3.3 per task.
- The best baseline is chosen on the evaluation seeds themselves, which favours the baselines.
- Verification and retry alone, with no tools, already gives about +0.12 over plain. Tool offload adds +0.09 to +0.15 on top of that.
- Removing the verifier from S1 costs 0.06-0.11 correctness.
- A 3-agent majority vote at 3x cost reaches only 0.70-0.75. S1 beats it by +0.14 to +0.20 at about 0.62-0.66x its cost.

**Improvement steps, each verified separately**
- **Step 1, learned tool selection:** it picks the right tool on 77-83% of compute tasks (static rule: 69-76%). It is still about 0.06 below oracle selection. My first selector was worse than S0; the fixes were designed on tune seeds 1-8, and two chosen hyper-parameters sit at the edge of the grid I searched.
- **Step 2a, tool-result cache:** per-task correctness is identical on all seeds in every set, so it only saves cost. It cuts 1.2-1.9 per task, with a hit rate of 21-28%. The saving scales with how many questions repeat, which is a world parameter (20-30% exact repeats here). At 0% repeats it still saves about 0.9.
- **Step 2b, verified-answer memo:** it cuts a further 1.6-2.5 per task and adds +0.005 to +0.008 correctness. At 0% repeats it does neither harm nor good.

**Controls**
- **No-compute tasks:** a tool on every task costs about -0.20 correctness and +14 cost. The learned selector skips the tool on 93-96% of those tasks. It still loses -0.005 to -0.008 correctness and +0.9 to +1.6 cost (about 9-16%). A ±1pp equivalence check holds in 3 of 4 set/generator cells and fails on confirm A.
- **Wrong tool always used:** correctness change is small (-0.004 to -0.017 in the main worlds), but cost is 3-4x. It costs -0.044 to -0.047 correctness on the no-compute control, where nothing can be verified.
- **60% misleading keywords:** S1 gains +0.19 to +0.25 over plain, versus +0.10 to +0.12 for the static rule.

**Where the lift disappears** (sensitivity runs on held seeds)
- With tool-call accuracy cut by 0.30 and no verifier coverage, the gain in generator A falls to +0.004 (not significant). In generator B it stays at +0.072.
- A flatter ungated error curve (slope x0.25) leaves +0.076 / +0.093.
- The verifier is assumed to see a clean machine-readable spec with probability 0.9 (A) / 0.8 (B). Getting such a spec is the hard part in practice.
- All error rates are assumptions, not measurements of a real LLM. Tool-call formulation errors are real string mutations run through the real tools, but who makes them, and how often, is seeded.

**To rerun everything** (about 8 minutes on the shared box):
`bash results/g13_run_all.sh`
The exact per-step rerun commands are in `results/g13_board_entry.md`.

READ-ONLY feasibility study (no installs, no downloads without audit, no code changes). Produce an HONEST written report: can we build our OWN AI agents with constantly-evolving, trainable neural pathways / neural networks — as opposed to the current setup (frozen Claude models + a learned Hebbian router/mesh around them). Write the report to C:\Users\mariu\neural-mesh\results\own-agents-feasibility.md and also return a concise summary.

Be rigorous and non-hype. Cover, with realistic numbers:
1. The key distinction: today the "intelligence" is a frozen large neural network (Claude) we cannot retrain; the router/mesh only learns to dispatch/retrieve. "Our own trainable agents" means training our own model weights. State this plainly up front.
2. The realistic options to actually own trainable weights, each with compute/data/cost/hardware reality for THIS machine (AMD Ryzen 7 8700F, 16 GB RAM, NVIDIA RTX 5060 Ti ~8-16 GB VRAM, CPU-first, no datacenter):
   a. Train a small model from scratch — what scale is feasible locally, and how weak it would be vs frontier models (be blunt: toy-to-small).
   b. Fine-tune an open-weight LLM locally (LoRA/QLoRA on a quantized 7B-14B) — what the GPU can realistically handle, what it buys, what data you'd need, rough time.
   c. Online / continual learning & plasticity (the "evolving neural pathways" idea): Hebbian/STDP, three-factor rules, elastic weight consolidation, replay — and the HONEST state of the art: catastrophic forgetting, stability-plasticity tradeoff, why continually-learning LLMs are an open research problem, not a product.
   d. Neuroevolution (NEAT / evolving topologies) and spiking nets — niche, small-scale only; where they're actually used.
   e. Adapter/memory-based "evolution without retraining" (LoRA hot-swap, retrieval memory) — the closest practical thing to "evolving" that works today, which is basically what our mesh/memory already does at the system level.
3. Honest verdict: what is actually achievable for the user now vs what is research-grade or infeasible; a credible step-by-step path if they want to pursue owning a trainable local model (e.g. LoRA-fine-tune a local open model + online-updatable adapters + our retrieval/router on top); and an explicit statement that any such model will be far weaker than Claude and will NOT autonomously self-improve into something smarter.
4. How this connects to what we've built: the router/mesh/memory already give measurable "gets better with use" at the dispatch/retrieval level without touching model weights; be clear about that boundary.
Cite that figures are rough/representative where you don't have exact numbers; don't invent benchmarks. No security-relevant downloads. Keep it to a tight, skimmable report with a clear verdict.
response:
Report written to C:\Users\mariu\neural-mesh\results\own-agents-feasibility.md. It is read-only research, with no installs, downloads or code changes. All figures are rough orders of magnitude from general knowledge, and no benchmarks were run.

**Verdict**
- Today the intelligence is Claude, a frozen model we cannot retrain. Our router, mesh and memory only learn dispatch, team assembly and retrieval, and no weights change.
- "Our own trainable agents" means owning and updating model weights. That is possible only at small scale, and the result is far weaker than Claude.

**Hardware correction:** nvidia-smi on this machine reports 8151 MiB for the RTX 5060 Ti, so the study assumes 8 GB VRAM, not 16.

**Options**
- **a. Train from scratch:** the practical ceiling is about 10M to 300M parameters (GPT-2-small class). The result is toy to small, so it is educational or single-purpose only, not an agent brain.
- **b. LoRA/QLoRA on an open model:** this is the one practical route. On 8 GB, 3B to 4B models are comfortable and 7B to 8B is tight but possible. A 14B model is not realistic here. It needs hundreds to a few thousand good examples, and a run takes minutes to a few hours. It changes style, format and narrow-task skill, not general intelligence. The main costs are evaluation and data quality.
- **c. Online/continual learning (Hebbian, STDP, three-factor, EWC, replay):** this works for small routing tables like ours. Catastrophic forgetting and the stability-plasticity tradeoff are unsolved at LLM scale, so continually learning LLMs are an open research problem, not a product. Live weight updates from raw traffic are also unsafe, because of noise, poisoning and silent regression.
- **d. Neuroevolution and spiking nets:** these are niche, small-scale tools. NEAT suits small control policies. Spiking nets suit neuromorphic and neuroscience work and give no advantage on CPU or GPU for language. The repo's `g8s_snn*` results are research probes, not an LLM path.
- **e. Adapters plus retrieval:** this is the closest thing to "evolving" that works today. It uses LoRA hot-swap with rollback, retrieval memory and routing, and it is what our mesh and memory already do at the system level.

**Explicit statements in the report**
- Any model we train will be far weaker than Claude.
- It will not autonomously self-improve into something smarter. Self-training loops without strong external verification tend to degrade.

**Suggested path (7 steps)**
1. Define one or two narrow tasks and build a held-out test set first.
2. Measure a prompted local model plus retrieval as the baseline.
3. Collect and audit data, checking license, privacy and Claude terms-of-service constraints.
4. Run QLoRA on a 3B to 8B model and keep it only if it clearly beats the baseline.
5. Plug it in as a versioned adapter behind the router, as one more agent with a health score.
6. Retrain in periodic batches with replay data and a regression gate, never continuously.
7. Treat EWC and model merging as experiments, not commitments.

**Caveat on our evidence:** the router and mesh results in `results/` come from a fixed synthetic simulation (hidden success probabilities, trap task types, drift, node failures, paired seeds). They show the learning rule works as designed. They are not proof of gains on real Claude workloads until validated on logged real outcomes. The report names that as the next honest step.

**Recommendation:** don't make "evolving neural agents" the goal. Validate the mesh on real outcomes, and add a small local QLoRA specialist only where a measured test shows it beats a prompted baseline. Keep adapters and retrieval as the "evolution" mechanism with human-gated retraining, and keep Claude as the reasoning engine.

response:
W15 / G14 follow-up triage is done and written to C:\Users\mariu\neural-mesh\results\g14_triage.md. It was read-only: I ran and installed nothing from ruvnet-clean or ruvnet-crates. The one registry file I opened is our own dependency, hnsw_rs-0.3.4. The report checks each of (a) to (e), with a verdict, a code-level description and a proposed experiment.

**Main conclusion.** For the verification and critic gate there is nothing worth importing. What the repos offer is already covered by results/g9_critic.log (flat and hierarchical SecondOpinion, evidence re-derivation, cross-source agreement, self-consistency, cascade, abstain-first, deterministic recompute). In g9 the evidence critics are within about 0.015 net of the oracle, so a better trigger has almost no headroom. Self-consistency loses at c=.05 (net .834 against .897 for no critic).

**Ranked proposals, all native reimplementations:**
1. **R2, hnsw_rs 0.3.4 reverse-edge bug.** I found a probable bug in the HNSW crate we depend on (`hnsw_rs = "0.3.4"`).
   - In `hnsw.rs:1229`, `reverse_update_neighborhood_simple` writes each reverse edge at `l_n = new_point.p_id.0`, the new point's top level, instead of the loop layer `l`.
   - For roughly 6% of points (level 1 or higher at M=16), the neighbours' layer-0 lists never receive the reverse edge, so layer-0 search can miss them.
   - ruvector-core's tests/hnsw_issue_773_* test files document this same bug and ship a patched hnsw_rs.
   - This is source reading only; I have not run it. It is consistent with our measured recall@10 of .96-.99 in research_board H2.
   - Experiment: query every stored vector against itself (k=1, ef=512) over at least 20 builds for N in {1k, 5k, 30k}, and compare with a local one-line-patched copy. Routing impact should be about zero on the flat default, but it could lose stored items in the tiered and casebased HNSW paths.
2. **R1, selective cascade trigger.** Escalate from MiniLM to a BGE rerank only when a trigger fires.
   - The trigger is the top1-top2 margin, or the set size from the split-conformal predictor in ruvector-core's `conformal_prediction.rs`, or softmax entropy.
   - It reuses the g1 fixtures A to D already on disk.
   - Metrics are hit@1 and MRR against fraction escalated, AURC, and conformal coverage when calibrated on A and tested on B, C and D.
   - I expect most of the roughly +.015-.02 cascade gain at about 30% escalation. Downstream routing gain should be near zero, since BGE gave 0 Holm wins in routing.
3. **R3, RRF (k=60) and RSF against the tuned-alpha hybrid in g1.** Hybrid raised hit@1 but dropped R@3 from .766 to .640. Expect an MRR tie and possibly a small R@3 recovery. It is about 20 lines.
4. **R4, odd quorum of 3 or more weak checkers with a correlation parameter** (from helix-verifier). Low value: independent weak checkers reach only about .65 recall against the evidence critic's .93-.96.
5. **R5, anytime-valid betting test for acting on critic flags**, in place of the Beta lower bound. This is the paired sequential test in `ruvector-typesafe-core`, and a tie is expected.

**Verdicts on the specific items:**
- **guardrail:** a structured-field policy checker with an OpenAI pass-through. It has no hallucination or claim checking.
- **helix-verifier / helix-pipeline:** the design is sound but already covered by g9, except for the quorum rule (R4). Its checker is only a trait stub.
- **prime-radiant "hallucination detection":** a weighted embedding-residual energy. Its confidence is a hand-set sigmoid, never fitted, and the demo uses constant vectors. It cannot see sibling-detail errors, which is g1's main error mode.
- **cognitum-gate:** the "e-value" is `mean(coherence)*100` in tilezero's `supergraph.rs`. The kernel uses fixed likelihood-ratio constants. Verdict: no.
- **SAFLA:**
  - The correction trigger is `performance_gap >= 0.2`.
  - The correction multiplies the learning rate by 1.1.
  - `expected_improvement` and `confidence_score` are constants.
  - Action recommendation is raw argmax over string-equal contexts.
  - `adaptive_safety_boundaries` raises the threshold when a constraint is violated, which is a design hazard.
  - There is no reusable trigger or calibration algorithm.
- **ruvector-gnn-rerank:** neighbour score averaging, with no GNN or min-cut. It is designed for i.i.d. quantisation noise, so on sibling confusion it behaves like Rocchio PRF, which lost about -.01 MRR in g1. Verdict: no.
- **ruvector-attention, attn-mincut, mincut:** need trained attention layers, which we lack. Verdict: no.
- **ruvector-core HNSW:** the defaults (m16, efc100, ef100) are the same as ours. It is a wrapper around hnsw_rs.
- **FACT:** an exact-key LRU cache, and ruvector-query-cache is a latency-only semantic cache. Verdict: no.
- **Self-consistency / selective prediction:** no such code exists anywhere in the 475 crates or the cloned repos. The only conformal code is the split-conformal predictor in ruvector-core. Its `calibrate` errors out if any true neighbour falls outside the top 100, which biases it toward easy sets.

**Security.** I saw no spawned processes, sockets or obfuscated code in the files I opened. Not audited and not to be built without review: prime-radiant (63k lines), veritas-nexus (68k) and SAFLA (43k lines of Python with FastAPI, deploy scripts and Dockerfiles).

**The defect.** `reverse_update_neighborhood_simple` (hnsw.rs line 1245) writes reverse edges at `l_n = new_point.p_id.0` (the new point's top level) instead of the loop layer `l`. I changed that one line in a vendored copy of the crate to `l as usize`.

**Measured over 200 builds per variant (120 iid, 80 clustered), M=16, ef_construction=200, cosine, sequential `insert_slice` as neural-mesh does:**
- **Unpatched:** every build loses items, measured as items that are not their own top-1 at ef=512, k=1.

  - Clustered data: 1.14-1.33%.
  - All 25,932 misses are level>=1 points (about 6.2% of items); there were zero misses on level-0 points.

- **Patched:** 0 misses, 0 in-degree-0 points and 0 unreachable points in all 200 builds.
- **Recall@10 vs brute force, patched minus unpatched, 95% CI over 20 seeds:**
  - 1k d32: +.0151 (ef 50) / +.0123 (ef 100) / +.0103 (ef 200).
  - 5k d384: +.0102 / +.0171 / +.0240.
  - 30k d32: +.0238 / +.0247 / +.0233, with ef=200 going from .9758 to .9991.
  - 30k d384: +.0018 / +.0058 / +.0086, but absolute recall is only about .52 in that regime.

response:
W19 (orchestration track O) is finished. Everything is a seeded simulation I wrote. It measures what decomposing, routing, retrieval, verification and learned stopping do to graded quality and cost in a world I defined. It says nothing about real LLMs or discovery.

**Files** (`src/*.rs` untouched, no commits). The main one is `results/g18_board_entry.md`, which holds the VERIFY REQUEST blocks (A–D), the negatives and the exact rerun commands.
- Code: `src/bin/g18_orch.rs`, `src/bin/g18_common/mod.rs`.
- Results in `results/`:
  - `g18_orch.{json,log}` (held 31-60)
  - `g18_orch_confirm61-90.{json,log}` (fresh seeds, same frozen tuning)
  - `g18_sens.{json,log}` and `g18_sens_confirm61-90.{json,log}` (sensitivity)

  - `g18_world_examples.txt`, `g18_check.log`, `g18_proposed_patch.md`

**Setup.** There are 15 worlds, fixed before any policy was run. Generator A is specialist pipelines (6 worlds), generator B is latent-factor agents with random DAGs (4 worlds), plus 5 controls. Each task has 3–6 dependent steps of four types, with hidden per-agent per-type competence, error propagation, recurring-project notes, a verifier with imperfect recall, and call costs.
- Baselines: 6 fair single-shot routers, plus `ss-warm+retr`, a single-shot router given the same notes as a control for the retrieval confound.
- Levels:
  - L1: decompose and route per step
  - L2: add retrieval
  - L3: add verify with retry/reroute
  - L4: add learned stopping
  - L5: add parallel fan-out
- Protocol: tuned on seeds 1-8, held 31-60, confirm 61-90, paired 95% t-CI, Holm per family.
- Determinism: two reruns of the 61-90 file are identical apart from `runtime_s`. Four unit tests pass.

**Which level moves quality** (graded H1500 vs the best fair single-shot, generator A | generator B; 61-90 matches within about .006):

| Level | Graded gain | Cost | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| L1 decompose + route | +.214 \| +.003 (ns) | unchanged | Real only when specialists differ by step type |
| L2 retrieval | +.080 \| +.067 more (all-correct +.275 \| +.103) | +.225/task | Largest generic lever; scales about linearly with the context-dependence parameter I set |
| L3 verify + retry/reroute | +.026 \| +.039 more (all-correct +.089 \| +.085) | +50% / +87% (pipe-main 4.73 → 6.97; lat-main 4.72 → 8.64) | Utility-negative once a unit of cost is worth more than about 0.05 quality; harmful with a noisy verifier |
| L4 learned stopping | quality ≈ L3 in A (+.001), −.008 in B | about 5.0 vs 7.0 in pipe-main | Checks per task drop from 5.19 to 0.63 |
| L5 parallel fan-out | 0 in all 15 worlds | none | Latency only: −0.33 in pipe-main, −2.1 in lat-main, −3.5 with independent steps |

- **Pure orchestration is smaller than it looks.** Against a single-shot router given the same notes, L2 gains +.29 in pipe-main but only +.02 in lat-main (other B worlds ns). L3 and L4 beat it Holm-significantly in 6/6 A and 4/4 B worlds.
- **Wins in both generators.** L2–L5 win against the best fair baseline in all 10 treatment worlds. L1 wins only in generator A.

**Controls and negatives**
- **L1 on a dominant agent:** L1 loses −.011 (Holm LOSS) in the dominant-agent, independent-step control. In the other controls it is ns, except the specialist, independent-step control (+.185).
- **Controls against baselines without notes:** L2–L5 "win" in every control against baselines that have no notes, because retrieval is the lever there, not decomposition.
- **Verification can hurt:**
  - In the poor-verifier world (`sig_v` .22), L3 is not better than L2 and all-correct drops −.065.
  - At `sig_v` .4, L3 is −.048 graded.
  - L4 is the best arm there.
- **Cheap, noisy verification:** part of L3's gain is best-of-k selection under agent noise, not error detection. In the equal-agents control L3 gains +.042 graded for +6.3 cost per task.
- **Rare errors, expensive checks:** L4 skips and cuts cost by 4.14 per task versus L3 with quality unchanged. At cv = 1.0 that skip is a prior rule, not learned. At cv .1/.3 it does learn, but still pays a small exploration tax versus no verification at all (utility −.002 to −.003).
- **Disclosure — tuning change:** my first run tuned L4 at utility weight mu = .1 and hit the never-verify grid edge. I changed only the L4 tuning utility (mu .03, wider grid), added metrics, and reran everything; worlds were untouched. Both runs are kept. The honest reading at mu = .1 is "don't verify at these prices".
- **Other limits:** the retrieval model is a stochastic stand-in, not the real index. No drift was tested for L4. Costs and parallelism are my own accounting.

**Proposals** (`results/g18_proposed_patch.md`): a step-level `run_plan` entry point, a `VerifyGate` for stopping, and a verifier/reroute contract. Of the library-level ideas, fan-out only justifies a scheduling helper.

Full report written to C:\Users\mariu\neural-mesh\results\market-research.md. Every figure is tagged PRIMARY (read on the source page), SECONDARY (third-party page or search summary), or ESTIMATE (my own arithmetic). I installed and cloned nothing.

**1. Market size**
- Menlo Ventures (2025-12-09) puts total enterprise gen-AI spend at $11.5B in 2024 and $37B in 2025, a 3.2x rise. Foundation-model API spend was $12.5B in 2025. These come from a survey of 495 US decision-makers, so they are estimates, not billing data.
- Menlo's earlier LLM-spend figure went from $3.5B in Nov 2024 to $8.4B in mid-2025.
- Gartner's AI spending is about $2.7T in 2026, but that is mostly hardware and infrastructure. Its "gen-AI models" line is $28.3B in 2026 and $51.6B in 2027 (SECONDARY; the Gartner page returned 403).
- Ten-year forecasts are for the broader gen-AI market, and they disagree widely: roughly $0.68T to $1.2T by 2035, at CAGRs of 31-41%. I would not cite any single one as the TAM.
- My own TAM/SAM framing (ESTIMATE): TAM is the API-token spend a router could touch, roughly $12.5B in 2025. SAM depends on an assumed 20-40% routable share, which is pure assumption and needs validation. I did not produce a SOM, because that needs pilot data.
- Sanity check: OpenRouter ARR is about $160M (Aug 2026, per Sacra) at a ~5% take. That implies roughly $3B of annualized spend flowing through it.

**2. Competition is strong and consolidating**
- OpenRouter raised $113M at about $1.3B in May 2026. Bloomberg reported on Aug 16 2026 that Stripe agreed to buy it for more than $7B.
- Portkey was acquired by Palo Alto Networks for about $140M (announced Apr 30 2026, closed May 29).
- Martian raised $9M in 2024. A blog says it is "nearing $1.3B" (unverified).
- Not Diamond has a thin raise (a blog reports about $2.3M pre-seed in late 2025). It already offers learned routing and prompt adaptation.
- RouteLLM is the open-source academic baseline. LiteLLM, Requesty, Cloudflare and Vercel gateways, and Bifrost/TrueFoundry cover gateway, fallback and caching. I did not verify Unify's current status.
- Memory specialists Mem0 (about $24M raised), Letta (about $10M) and Zep overlap the shared-memory half.
- Fallback and failover are table stakes, not a differentiator. Our only plausible edge is bundling learned routing with shared agent memory. That is an untested hypothesis, and the technique has public prior art.

**3. Savings**
- Vendor and authors' own claims: RouteLLM reports over 85% cost reduction on MT-Bench at 95% of GPT-4 quality. On MMLU and GSM8K it reports 45% and 35%. Martian claims 20-97% and Not Diamond claims 20-40%.

**4. Segments and pain**
- Target segments, in order of fit: AI-native startups, agent-platform builders, then large enterprises.
- Cost pain is supported by Menlo's 3.2x spend growth and by Gartner's forecast that over 40% of agentic projects will be cancelled by 2027, citing escalating costs (SECONDARY).
- Claims that 73% of enterprises overran AI cost projections, or that agents use 5-30x more tokens per task, come from blogs and are unverified.

  - gpt-6-luna: $0.10/$0.50
  - gpt-5.4-mini: $0.75/$4.50

- Google (SECONDARY, summarizer):

  - 3.7/3.8 Flash: $0.75/$3.75, rising to $1.50/$7.50 on 2027-01-01
  - 3.5 Flash-Lite: $0.30/$2.50

- Anthropic's 4.7+ tokenizer produces about 30% more tokens for the same text, so per-token comparisons across vendors understate real cost differences.

W20 (SONA-A) final report. All numbers are SYNTHETIC-until-validated-on-real-traffic. src/*.rs is untouched; I only added files under src/bin and results.

**Verdict.** SonaPlus is improved only in one narrow, author-built class of worlds. Evidence-gated, set-level (conjunction) pattern memory, placed behind the unchanged `defaults::recommended_guard()`, beats the best fair baseline where the best agent depends on feature conjunctions. It is harmless in my 6 control worlds. It is a loss in additive many-surface-form worlds. Learned anchors, kNN blending, consolidation and credit-with-the-SONA-estimator add nothing measurable over simpler alternatives in normal feedback.

**Mechanism that works ("K-full").** `HybridInner` trains hebbian-robust and `KeyedMemory` on every outcome. The decision comes from the memory only when its set-level evidence for the task's key reaches `min_w`; otherwise hebbian-robust decides. Evidence is the exact key-set pattern weight plus a Jaccard-weighted blend of the k=3 nearest patterns. Seeds 1-8 tuning chose min_w=3. The gate is what makes it safe in controls.

**Results (Holm, paired 95% CI, vs best of the 6 spec baselines, H2000):**

| Block | Worlds with Holm WIN | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| 31-60 | conj-clean +0.038, conj-noisy +0.020, conjT-clean +0.064, shortmod-traps +0.034, shortmod-clean +0.049 | conjT-noisy +0.003 n.s. |
| 61-90 (fresh, frozen tuning) | same 5 worlds: +0.038, +0.020, +0.068, +0.038, +0.054 | |
| 91-120 (fresh, post-hoc min_w=8) | conj-clean +0.041, conj-noisy +0.021, conjT-clean +0.065, shortmod-clean +0.043 | shortmod-traps +0.017 n.s. |

- **Direct K-full minus guarded-safe (Holm wins/losses of 75 cells):** 20/7 (31-60) and 24/6 (61-90). With min_w=8 on 91-120: 18/3.
- **Controls:** no Holm loss vs the best baseline in any of var-single, traps(main), correct-keywords, many-topics(16), sim-random, sim-notraps, in all blocks. The ungated memory is not harmless: it loses in correct-keywords and sim-notraps, although its conjunction wins are larger.
- **Ablation (normal feedback has no reuse signal, so no confound):** K[anchors+hebbian], which is the same guard and anchors with no pattern memory, is equal to guarded-safe and has 0 wins in all blocks. Per-feature (unigram) pattern memory has 5 wins / 22 losses vs best-of-6; K-full minus it is 28 wins / 1 loss on 31-60 and 30 wins / 0 losses on 61-90. Only the set-level key helps, which re-confirms the D7 finding for per-feature memory.
- **Weak feedback, all arms fed the same reuse signal:** K-full[reuse] beats the strict pool only in weak-shortmod-traps (+0.044 / +0.056 at H2000). The large gains vs raw-fed baselines (e.g. +0.106 in weak-var-traps) are the reuse signal, as in D7.

**Negatives, stated plainly.**
- The wins exist only where I built conjunction structure. Five winning worlds come from two generators, not real data.
- conjT-*, var-wide and shortmod-* were added after seeing round-1/round-4 results.
- Frozen K-full loses 0.011-0.017 at H2000 in var-traps, var-clean and var-wide-traps (Holm p ≤ 1e-3 in both fresh blocks).
- min_w=8 reduces that loss to about 0.00-0.005 on 31-60, 61-90 and 91-120. It is a post-hoc one-factor choice made after the sensitivity table; var-clean is still a Holm loss of -0.005 on 91-120.
- In the trap-keyword conjunction worlds (conjT-*), K-full loses early (H100-H250) by 0.04-0.10 to eps-greedy/hebbian-robust. That is the keyword guard (guarded-safe has the same deficit), not the memory.
- **Learned anchors:** neutral in normal feedback (K-full minus no-anchors: 1 win / 0 losses and 3 / 1). Under sparse feedback they add +0.017 to +0.028 at H2000 (4 wins / 0 losses in both blocks). Clustering purity is 1.00 in `--diag-anchors`, but permissive thresholds cost 0.002-0.006 at H2000 in controls. The oracle-anchor diagnostic shows headroom for semantic anchors, which `knowledge.rs` could supply with real embeddings; I did not test that.
- **Consolidation:** with 16 patterns instead of 1161, importance-merge keeps ~45% of the memory's gain (0.5018 vs 0.5325 uncapped, guarded-safe 0.4765), while LRU/FIFO keep none (0.476-0.479). It never beats uncapped.
- **Trajectory credit** (posterior blame split in session worlds): a large generic gain for every router (guarded-safe 0.535 → 0.712 in sess-traps at H2000). The SONA pattern-memory estimator is worse than a plain per-feature estimator (0 wins / 10-12 losses), and no K arm beats the credit-fed baselines. This is not SONA-specific.

**Process.** The worlds and candidate went through 5 rounds, each with changes made after seeing 31-60 results; all five rounds are listed in the board entry (rounds 1-4 logs kept in `results/` but not reproducible by the final binary). 61-90 was frozen-tuning fresh seeds, and 91-120 was an extra fresh block.

- **Data:** synthetic only. The primary case is N=96 channels; N=32, 130 and 256 (Python) and 32, 96 and 130 (Rust) are sensitivity runs.
- **Python:** lag history H=10, so ridge p=960. Warmup is 500 calls, then 30 reps × 20,000 timed calls per row, GC off inside timed loops.
- **Rust:** the arena API only takes whole trials (T=300), so per-step figures are amortised over the call. Warmup is 3 passes plus 200 one-step calls, then 30 reps × 24 trials.
- **Repeatability:** the whole protocol was run twice, and run-to-run spread is about 5–10%.
- **Timer floor:** Windows timers resolve to 100 ns, so Rust ridge at 0.1–0.4 µs is only "sub-microsecond".

**Measured numbers (N=96, µs per step).**

| Decoder | p50 | p95 | p99 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Python ridge, 1-step `predict` | 3.4 | 3.8 | 4.8 |
| Python Kalman streaming step | 3.9 | 4.4 | 4.8 |
| Python ridge + lag-window assembly | 4.5 | 5.1 | 5.4 |
| numpy GRU cell h=64 (proxy only) | 22.4 | 25.7 | 38.9 |
| Rust ridge | 0.24 | 0.47 | 0.52 |
| Rust Kalman | 397 | 455 | 499 |
| Rust GRU reservoir h=32 | 10.4 | 13.0 | 18.7 |
| Rust GRU reservoir h=64 | 23.2 | 29.1 | 39.3 |

- **Python batch (T=2000):** ridge 1.43 µs/step (about 698k steps/s), Kalman loop 2.76 µs/step (about 362k steps/s).
- **Rust throughput:** ridge about 3.2M steps/s, Kalman about 2,500, GRU h=32 about 90k.
- **Rust Kalman at N=130:** 921 µs p50, 1,152 µs p99.
- **Python Kalman vs N:** the streaming step stays flat, 3.9 to 4.2 µs from N=32 to N=256.

**Hot-path claims.**
- **Algorithmic delay dominates:** confirmed. The delay terms are derived, not timed: a 20 ms bin adds 10 ms mean age, and α=0.9 smoothing adds 9 bins = 180 ms (numerically verified). Python decode is about 0.02% of a 20 ms bin. Even the slowest decoder (Rust Kalman, N=130) is 4.6% of a bin.
- **Python Kalman loop as a hot path:** refuted as a latency problem. It costs about 4 µs per step and barely changes with N, so it is interpreter overhead (inferred from that flat scaling, not profiled).
- **GRU whole-sequence only:** confirmed by reading the code (`predict_seqs` takes `[S,T,N]`, no per-step API). It is not confirmed by timing, since torch was not measurable. The only GRU numbers are the Rust fixed-gate reservoir and the numpy proxy.
- **New finding:** the Rust `arena-core` Kalman is the slowest decoder measured. It recomputes covariance and inverts a dense N×N matrix every step, and scales superlinearly with N (24 µs at N=32, 397 µs at N=96, 921 µs at N=130). That is about 100× slower per step than the Python steady-state Kalman.

**Speed story for the website.** "On a Ryzen 7 8700F desktop, single thread, synthetic 96-channel data, our research-grade linear decoder takes about 3.5 µs per decode step (p99 under 5 µs) and our Kalman step about 4 µs, compute only. In a closed loop, binning and smoothing set the delay, not the decoder. Research and simulation only; not a medical device."

Separately, the only citable external figure is NDT at 3.9 ms (arXiv:2108.01210). It is a published preprint with a different setup and is not a head-to-head. The doc says never to pair it with ours as a ranking.

**Optimization lever.** By the brief's own gate (decode plus features above 10% of the bin, i.e. above 2 ms at 20 ms), nothing measured warrants a rewrite. If one lever is pulled, make it the Rust Kalman. Replace the per-step N×N inverse with the equivalent Woodbury/information form (a 2×2 inverse, since R is diagonal), or precompute the steady-state gain as m1lib does. Write the parity test first, change only that function, re-run `bench_baseline` on the same machine and seeds, and require the leak and recovery tests to pass. The doc also lists the ADR proposal for later (pytest-benchmark or asv, criterion, torch GRU, WASM via Playwright, fixed-arrival-schedule run, real-data fixtures).

Raw outputs are `py-bench-run1.json`, `py-bench-run2.json`, `rust-bench-run1.txt` and `rust-bench-run2.txt`, and the Python harness is `nf_bench_py.py`, all in the scratchpad.

You are the latency R&D team on NeuroForge Bio. Working copy: C:\Users\mariu\AppData\Local\Temp\claude\C--Users-mariu\8f3352b3-40ab-4151-abc9-d1de1978973c\scratchpad\neuroforge\ . Mandate: scientifically study how to push END-TO-END closed-loop decode latency toward <10 ms, and tell the truth about what's achievable. Use WebSearch for current literature; cite sources. Honesty: no fabricated results, no "we beat everyone" claims; distinguish measured vs theoretical vs literature.

FRAME IT CORRECTLY (this is the key insight): decoder COMPUTE is already sub-µs–µs. End-to-end latency is dominated by (a) temporal windowing — integrating spikes/power over a window puts the window center ~half-window in the past; (b) acquisition packetization + bus/network jitter (2–10 ms); (c) software overhead — GIL/GC freezes, lock contention, heap reallocation; (d) non-causal/bidirectional model layers and output smoothing (Kalman/low-pass phase lag). So the levers are algorithmic/architectural, not "faster matrix math."

DELIVER (write to scratchpad\neuroforge-latency-rnd.md):
1. A LATENCY BUDGET: decompose end-to-end delay into its terms with realistic numbers (cite literature for acquisition/packetization and for reported closed-loop BCI latencies). Show where the ~180 ms in our current config comes from and which terms are controllable vs fundamental.
2. METHODS to cut each controllable term, with evidence: causal-only models (no bidirectional), overlapping short windows + information-preserving features, exponential/causal smoothing with bounded lag, lock-free streaming + pre-allocation + pinned real-time threads, SIMD, event/spike-driven updates, latent-manifold / low-dimensional causal decoders. For each: expected ms saved and the accuracy risk.
3. THE WINDOW/ACCURACY FRONTIER: run a small SIMULATED study (synthetic or the repo's existing decoders) showing decode accuracy vs window size as you shrink the window toward <10 ms of integration — quantify the tradeoff honestly. Build to scratchpad\nf-target-rnd if you compile Rust; no new crates without an audit note; mind RAM.
4. HONEST VERDICT on "write our own programming language / compiler": evaluate it against Rust/C++ + lock-free + SIMD + RT scheduling. Expected conclusion: a general new language is NOT worth it; at most a narrow codegen/DSL for the fixed pipeline. Say so plainly with reasoning; if you find a genuine niche, justify it.
5. A prioritized research + engineering roadmap to credibly approach <10 ms end-to-end, with the explicit caveat about the fundamental windowing/accuracy tradeoff and that sub-10 ms may cost accuracy. This doubles as the CTO architecture recommendation for the investor pack.
Return a concise summary with the latency budget and the verdict.
response:
Report written to `C:\Users\mariu\AppData\Local\Temp\claude\C--Users-mariu\8f3352b3-40ab-4151-abc9-d1de1978973c\scratchpad\neuroforge-latency-rnd.md`. Study code and results are in `...\scratchpad\nf-latency-rnd\`: `window_frontier.py`, `frontier_results.json`, `lagpeak.py`, `lagpeak_results.json`, `micro.rs`. No repo file was touched, no crates were added, and I used no network beyond web search/fetch. The only compile was `rustc` 1.95.0 run directly, with no cargo.

Evidence caveat: every literature figure comes from search-result summaries. Two Nature fetches were blocked by redirects, so no primary paper was read in full. I found no primary source for acquisition packet latency (Cerebus/Neuropixels) or for display latency, so your 2-10 ms acquisition range is plausible but unverified. The report tags each number as measured, derived, simulated, literature or estimate.

**Latency budget (current config: 20 ms bins, alpha 0.9)**
- **Smoothing dominates.** Exponential smoothing at alpha 0.9 adds a group delay of 9 bins, which is 180 ms (derived). That is about 86-90% of the roughly 200-215 ms total.
- **The other terms:**
  - bin age: 10 ms
  - acquisition: about 1-10 ms (estimate)
  - display: 8-17 ms at 60 Hz
  - jitter: affects tails only
  - decode compute: about 0.004 ms
- **Compute is negligible.** Our Rust microbenchmark measured a 2x960 readout at 1.1 µs in f64, at or below the 100 ns timer floor in f32 with 8-lane accumulation, and about 0.6 µs per 1 ms sample for the 96-channel EMA feature bank.
- **Controllable:** smoothing, window width, packet size and transport, display or output path, causal-only models, allocation, locking and pinning.
- **Fundamental:** the window/SNR trade-off and the human visuomotor loop.

**Window/accuracy frontier (synthetic simulation, 3 seeds, ridge, 96 channels, 3 Hz latent velocity)**
- **R2 against the current velocity by window width:**

| Window (ms) | 5 | 10 | 20 | 40 | 80 | 160 | 320 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| R2 | 0.53 | 0.69 | 0.81 | 0.87 | 0.83 | 0.59 | 0.25 |

  Below about 20 ms the trade is roughly one-for-one accuracy for latency.
- **More channels buy window size.** At 256 channels R2 is 0.86 at 10 ms and 0.75 at 5 ms. Higher SNR gives similar gains.
- **Output smoothing:** R2 is 0.81 with none, 0.86 at alpha 0.3 (8.6 ms delay), and 0.46 at alpha 0.9 (180 ms). Light smoothing helps; the current setting is deeply harmful.
- **Predict-ahead** to cancel a fixed pipeline delay costs roughly 0.02-0.03 R2 per 10 ms up to 20 ms, then falls off steeply.
- **Multiscale features** (fine recent bins, coarse older ones) do not beat a boxcar at the same short history. Their gain is that long history adds no latency (R2 0.876 versus 0.867 for the best boxcar).
- **What the simulation is not:** a toy with linear, stationary tuning, no neural lead, no closed-loop adaptation and no real data. The curve shape is the finding, not the absolute R2.

**Under 10 ms:** it is only possible if all of the following hold:
- a window of about 5-10 ms
- acquisition packets of 1-2 ms or less (unverified for any hardware)
- a 240 Hz or direct output path
- no output smoothing

The budget then totals about 5.5-9 ms. It is a hardware/SNR/accuracy trade-off, not a software-speed one. Closed-loop literature favours 20-50 ms bins, and the human loop is much slower than 10 ms, so it may not be worth chasing for cursor control.

**Verdict on a new language or compiler: no.** The decoder already runs at about 1 µs against a millisecond budget, so a compiler could save at most about 0.01%. The real jitter fixes are plain engineering: preallocated buffers, lock-free ring buffers, core pinning, PREEMPT_RT Linux, and restructuring reductions for SIMD (we saw 10x from the restructure alone). The only defensible niche is a narrow code generator for the fixed pipeline, with worst-case-execution-time certificates. It is only justified if an FPGA or on-implant target appears, so prototype it as a Rust macro or build-script template first.

**Roadmap highlights**
- **P0:** remove alpha 0.9 smoothing, instrument the budget with per-stage timestamps and an effective-lag metric, and add a causality guard test in CI.
- **P1:**
  - measure acquisition and output on a real or replayed device
  - rerun the frontier on MC_Maze and MC_RTT under the repo's leak guards
  - build a streaming Rust runtime: preallocated, f32, SIMD-friendly readout with a steady-state or Woodbury Kalman (this also fixes the 397 µs per-step inverse in the repo's `arena-core` Kalman)
- **P2:** an RT Linux deployment profile, a latent-manifold/SBP/more-channels study, and predictive compensation.
- **P3:** a closed-loop user study, and codegen only if a hardware target appears.

The report also has safe investor wording and a do-not-say list. Notably, do not quote the roughly 10 ms speech-synthesis figure or the NDT 3.9 ms figure until a coder reads the primary papers.

2. **Hybrid sparse plus dense retrieval fused with Reciprocal Rank Fusion, reranking only the top 20 candidates with a cheap scorer (about 0.6).**
   - A cross-encoder reranker typically adds around 100-300 ms per query, which would swamp a sub-millisecond lookup. Use it only if end-to-end accuracy visibly rises.
   - Judge on end-to-end task accuracy, not recall alone; the earlier MiniLM-vs-BGE result already showed recall gains don't always carry through.
3. **Offline warm-start priors for the bandit (about 0.45).** Expect gains in the first 250-500 tasks that fade by about 2000, matching the existing keyword-prior result. It can lose under distribution shift.
4. **Retrieval-augmented routing with an abstain gate (about 0.4).**
   - The earlier case-based router was rejected, so this is a deliberate revisit.
   - It differs by adding the abstain gate and real semantic embeddings.
   - Expect a tie unless similar tasks actually predict the best agent.
5. **Query-embedding and result caching (about 0.7 for latency, zero change in quality).** Guaranteed latency win on repeated tasks; invalidate entries on memory writes.
6. **Multi-bit RaBitQ-style codes as a scan stage, with full-precision rerank (about 0.5 on bytes, tie on recall).** Worth doing only if the shared store grows past roughly 1e5-1e6 vectors; at small sizes a flat scan is already fast.
7. **Verbalized Sampling for creative-tagged tasks only (about 0.35).** The paper (arXiv 2510.01171) reports 1.6-2.1x diversity without hurting factual accuracy or safety. It needs a non-inferiority test on the correctness worlds.
8. **Router-state efficiency (about 0.3, likely a tie).** CompactRouter already took most of the bytes. The cheap real win is computing each task embedding once and sharing it, which should leave decisions bit-identical. Int8 quantization and a distilled lookup table are likely ties on quality.
9. **MAP-Elites or novelty-search archives for creative output (about 0.15).** Build the simple baseline first: best-of-k with embedding-distance dedup. Expect the archive to tie against it, so only build it if dedup shows a measurable diversity gain.

**Things I'd advise against:**
- Router-level Thompson/UCB for creative tasks. It was already tried and tied, and exploring among agents doesn't make an LLM's output more novel.
- Learned deferral or confidence-token routers. They need labeled training and are the rejected learned-router idea in another form.
- Learned indexes. I found no strong evidence they beat HNSW for high-dimensional vectors at our scale.
- RouteLLM-style routers. The reported savings are for a specific strong/weak model pair, not for choosing among agents.

**Suggested order:** the two engineering wins first (shared embedding, caching), then hybrid retrieval, then the verification gate, then warm-start priors.

**Validation rule throughout:** tune on seeds 1-30 and report on 61-90, with Holm correction. Use the existing no-synergy and randomized worlds as negative controls. Count verifier and rerank cost as a cost, so a gain that doubles the call count is a loss.

| System | F1@3 | MRR | hit@1 |
|---|---|---|---|
| dense+spell | .626 | .946 | .915 |
| hybrid (z-fusion, alpha .8) | .552 | .961 | .943 |
| RRF | .457 | .940 | .905 |
| RSF | .557 | .960 | .940 |
| rerank-logit | .654 | .960 | .940 |

- RRF and RSF need an absolute admission floor; I put it on the dense cosine, so they collapse onto the dense arm. Other floors were not tried.
- Post-hoc changes, disclosed in the entry: the raw-dense arm was added after pass 1 (pass-1 files kept as `h2_route_pass1.*`), the strict "adds over spell" rule, and the ±.01 non-inferiority margin (copied from g16). The literal pre-declared rule is reported unchanged.
