**Changes to `src/compact.rs` (all opt-in, defaults unchanged)**
- **Row layout:** rows are now sorted by feature id (no separate slot index) and the agent mask is `ceil(n/8)` bytes. The agent limit goes from 64 to 128, and runs of up to 64 agents pay nothing for that.
- **Bounded vocabulary:** `Vocab::bounded` / `SharedVocab::bounded` / `vocab_cap`. Lowest-hit non-keyword strings are evicted in batches, keyword strings are pinned, and recycled ids carry a generation so stale rows in other brains can never match a new string.
- **Row cap:** `max_rows` evicts the rarest rows first, using decayed guard-evidence mass.
- **12-bit cells:** `Fx12` and `Q12`, really bit-packed.
- **Binary state:** `to_bytes` / `from_bytes` (exact round trip), a state-only form `state_bytes`, and `BrainPool` for cold brains.
- **Speed work:** one-pass `decide` and a rounding/division-free u16 encode/decode.

**One existing test changed:** `byte_accounting_is_exact_for_the_u16_layout` now asserts the new per-row layout. The other 10 R3 tests are unchanged and green. The u16 representation is also no longer bit-identical to R3's because of the rounding change. The f64/f32 instances still match the shipped router exactly (diff 0.0000, identical at 3 to 128 agents).

**Equivalence**
- **Protocol:** TOST at ±0.005, with a 95% CI and Holm across the 8 worlds. The worlds are the 3 sim worlds, big-32, big-32 long-tail, big-32 open-stream, big-64 and big-128.
- **Stage 1 (declared before running, pooled 31-90 + power 91-250):** even the u16/q16 baseline could not be certified at 64 and 128 agents. At 64 agents the diff was +0.0027 [-0.0002, +0.0056]; I put this down to power.
- **Stage 2 (declared after stage 1, fresh seeds 91-450, n=360):** u16/q16 is certified in all 8 worlds, so lifting the limit to 128 agents is supported. Seeds 91-250 were already used in stage 1; the untouched seeds 251-450 alone also pass.
- **Pass:** hash32 (identical to u16/q16 here) and the bounded vocabulary at every fraction down to keywords-only.
- **Fail:**
  - **u8 weights:** -0.0105 in sim-fixed, a real loss.
  - **u12 weights and 12-bit counts:** not equivalent at 32+ agents. u12/q12 is non-inferior, but 12-bit changes behaviour (u12/q12 +0.0120 at 64 agents) and saves only 9-17% of bytes. Why is untested; my guess is that rounding stalls the weight decay.
  - **Row caps:** -0.02 to -0.055 in the sim worlds, and -0.0086 at a 50% cap in big-32. They only work in the long-tail and open worlds.
  - **Random eviction instead of value-based:** far worse, e.g. -0.013 in long-tail versus -0.0012 with value-based eviction.
  - **Cell pruning:** only a 1-3% saving at settings that pass.
- **Biggest caveat:** the tail tokens in my worlds are pure noise by construction, so a keywords-only vocabulary being harmless here is an upper bound, not evidence for real traffic. The row-cap results are the control: when evicted features carry signal, it costs quality.
- **Shared bounded vocabulary, 240 brains over one vocab:** certified at 95% in the long-tail and open worlds, but only at 90% in big-32 (CI [-0.0051, +0.0055]), so it fails my 95% rule there.

**Bytes saved**
- **Layout alone (same state):** owned bytes per trained brain drop 8% for sim-fixed, 10% for big-32 and 22% for long-tail.
- **Bounded vocabulary (largest lever that passes everywhere):** brain plus private vocabulary shrinks 74-89% in the long-tail and open worlds.
- **Binary state:** 54-62% smaller than the R3 JSON and about the size of the in-memory brain (JSON was ~2.2x memory). The round trip is exact in every world.
- **Agents per GiB:** the table shows shipped f64 router, R3 private, R4 shared vocab, R4 with a 5%-hot pool; units are thousands.

| World | f64 router | R3 private | R4 shared vocab | R4 5%-hot pool |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| sim-fixed | 66.8k | 189k | 477k | 719k |
| big-32 | 4.36k | 24.0k | 56.0k | 60.2k |
| long-tail | 572 | 4.28k | 17.5k | 21.7k |
| big-64 | 2.53k | 22.5k | 45.9k | 49.0k |
| big-128 | 1.38k | n/a | 39.3k | 40.7k |

- **Open world:** 414 → 3.85k agents/GiB, because the unbounded shared vocabulary dominates (~57.7 MB for 240 brains).
- **Cold pool:** reloads and decisions are bit-exact against all-hot twins, with a median reload of 5.6 µs (sim) up to about 100 µs (long-tail) and 30 µs at big-32. It only gains 1.0-1.5x over keeping the shared vocabulary hot, and every-decision churn is 8 to 90 times slower, so spill only pays for brains that sit idle.

**Latency**
- **Method:** ns per decision, minimum over 21 interleaved reps, against a verbatim copy of the old R3 compact. The box was shared at 9-80% background CPU, so only the ratios mean anything.
- **vs R3:** the declared +10% criterion is met in all 7 worlds where R3 exists. R4 comes out at 0.85-0.99 of R3's ns.
- **vs f64:** R4 is 0.47 to 0.24 of the f64 router's ns from 6 to 64 agents, and 0.18 at 128 agents (1.9 µs versus 10.6 µs).
- **Where the speed-up comes from:** the one-pass `decide` and the rounding-free encode/decode. The sorted-row layout alone was +8 to +35% slower than R3 before those fixes.
- **Other variants vs R3:** u12/q12 packed is 0.99-1.22 and the 50% row cap is up to about 2x in the 6-agent worlds.

**Recommendation (nothing made default):**
- Keep the new layout and the 128-agent limit.
- Use a bounded or shared vocabulary for open token streams.
- Use hash32 when feature names need not be persisted.
- Use binary state for save/load.
- Do not set row caps below the signal-row count, and do not use 8/12-bit cells or cell pruning.

R4-B3 / h6 (memory-reduction track) is finished. Everything is synthetic-until-validated, nothing in src/*.rs was edited, and the box stayed within the RAM cap (1e6 gate run peaked at 2,254 MB working set). Compression of the knowledge store held downstream quality; the cheapest safe options are block-fp16 and int8. The full write-up, with exact rerun commands per block, is `results/h6_board_entry.md`.

**Files** (all under C:\Users\mariu\neural-mesh)
- `src/bin/h6_store.rs`: `check`, `loop` and `loopbase` modes.
- `src/bin/h6_docq.rs`: `docq` and `ctx` modes.

- Proposals go in `results/h6_proposed_patch.md` (block-fp16/int8 `FlatIndex` tier, size-gating function, exact-duplicate suppression on ingest).

**Protocol (declared before running)**
- TOST margin was ±0.01 on H2000 success, against the f32 flat store of the same policy.
- Policies were R0 (g1 default retrieval) and the frozen g16 FINAL, across all 8 worlds including sibling-heavy (sib16, sib64) and the controls (ctl-irrel, ctl-oneoff).
- Corpus A seeds 31-60 was held-out; corpus B seeds 61-90 was a confirm re-run of the identical arms. Nothing was tuned.
- `h6_store check` shows my copied engine matches `g16::run` exactly (max difference 0).
- Holm correction was applied over the 8 worlds per arm.
- Retrieval itself is worth +0.077 to +0.101 H2000 in sib16/rand16 and only +0.008 in weakid50. So ±0.01 is a weak equivalence claim in sib64 and weakid50; the CIs are in the json.

**Results: bytes saved per quality held**

| Store | Row bytes (f32 = 1872) | Quality held? |
|---|---|---|
| block-fp16 | 1152 (-38 %) | Identical decisions in the loop (diff exactly 0.0000, both policies, both corpora). 0 doc-level loss in 8 doc/chunk sets. |
| int8 (f32 or int8 query) | 724 (-61 %) | TOST-equivalent in all 4 policy x corpus cells. Worst-world H2000 diff -0.0022. Doc recall@10 0.995-0.999. |
| f16 | 1104 (-41 %) | Equivalent in all 4 cells. |
| turbovec 4-bit + f32 rerank 4x, f32 copy off-RAM | 532 in RAM + 1536 off-RAM | Equivalent in all cells; doc recall 1.000. Needs the f32 copy somewhere, see the disk cost below. |

- The 320 B sparse tf-idf part of each hybrid row is not compressed, which is why int8 saves 61 % of a row rather than 75 %.
- At loop scale the store is only 2000 rows (3.7 MB), so absolute savings are tiny. Percentages scale linearly with store size.
- Retrieval gain kept: 99-100 % for block-fp16, int8, f16 and rerank arms.

**Honest negatives**
- turbovec 2/3/4-bit without rerank is not a safe scan. Doc recall@10 vs f32 is 0.94-0.985, so it fails a ±0.01 bar everywhere. FINAL fails equivalence in at least one world on 4-bit (corpus B), 3-bit (corpus B) and 2-bit (A and B).
- Many "NO" cells are inconclusive rather than proven harm: CIs straddle zero and the chaotic loop trajectory is noisy.
- Anchor-summary rows (-94 % rows) are not equivalent for FINAL (-0.0078 in sib16/drift on corpus B, CI excludes 0); retuned thresholds were worse.
- Exact-duplicate suppression in the vote loop (-90 % rows) is neutral for R0, but FINAL sib16 on B is inconclusive (-0.0085, CI crossing 0).
- Adaptive k and a byte budget save no store bytes in the vote. k≥3 is equivalent; k≤2 and adaptive k are inconclusive for FINAL on corpus B.
- turbovec-style rerank needs the f32 copy in RAM, which erases the saving. With the f32 copy on cold disk (`FILE_FLAG_NO_BUFFERING`, queue depth 1, which is the real SSD cost) it costs +4.5 ms per query at 4x and 18 ms at 16x.
- My own RaBitQ-style 1-bit code is slower than flat f32 at 1e5-1e6 and recalls 0.18-0.40 raw; that is an implementation result, not a verdict on RaBitQ. turbovec stands in as the multi-bit option.

**Context compression (doc level)**
- The F1 knee is k=2 at about 650 chars. This is by construction, because each concept has 2 relevant docs.
- Versus k=3 that is -33 % chars with F1 +0.013 (A) / +0.021 (B).
- A byte budget equals k here because docs are about 327 chars each.
- Adaptive drop is below fixed k=2.
- Suppressing exact-duplicate docs gives F1@k=2 +0.036 (A) / +0.025 (B) with 30 % re-ingested duplicates, and removes 23 % of rows.

**Size gating (synthetic 1e4 / 1e5 / 1e6, d=384, one thread)**
- 1e6 latencies were inflated about 1.4x by box load.
- Flat f32 p50: 0.47 ms at 1e4, 5.2 ms at 1e5, 67 ms at 1e6. Block-fp16: 0.31 / 3.7 / 44 ms. int8 + rerank (f32 in RAM): 0.15 / 1.6 / 18.7 ms. turbovec 4-bit + rerank (f32 in RAM): 0.24 / 1.2 / 14 ms; recall stays 1.000.
- Crossover: flat f32 is right up to roughly 2e4 vectors (p50 ≤ 1 ms), and up to 1e5-3e5 at a 5-20 ms budget when RAM is not binding. Compression forces itself on latency before RAM; 1e6 x 1536 B is 1.5 GB, which fits the 3 GB cap.
- The size-gating rule agrees with the measured grid in 27/27 cells. About 20 of those are trivial f32-or-NONE picks, and the 3e5 row and anything above 1e6 are model output, not measurement. HNSW/IVF was not in the grid; a ≤1 ms budget at ≥1e5 returns "needs an ANN graph".

**Recommended store configuration** (opt-in, defaults unchanged)
- Use block-fp16 as the free tier and int8 when you need -61 % per row.
- Above about 1e5, add an exact rerank with the f32 copy in RAM, because int8 alone recalls 0.961 at 1e6.
- Reserve f32-on-disk for when RAM actually binds and about 5 ms of extra latency is acceptable.
- Use 2-3 context docs, and suppress exact-duplicate docs before retrieval.
- Avoid summary rows, adaptive-k for byte savings, and turbovec without rerank.
- Re-measure on real traffic before any default changes.

- Seeds are resampled worlds, not independent corpora.

| Config | B/vec | M vec/GB |
|---|---|---|

| turbovec 4-bit | 196 | 5.1 |

| HNSW | 5.1-8.7 KB | 0.11-0.2 |

- turbovec 3-bit is stored at the 4-bit footprint. g15's 148 B was nominal, not measured.
- SSD-backed exact rerank (`FileRows`, direct I/O):
  - Cost: 70 µs per row single-threaded. A shared handle stays at 14k rows/s; one handle per thread scales to 113k rows/s at 8 threads.
  - What it buys: turbovec 4-bit with x4 rerank keeps 196-207 B RAM/vec (4.8-5.1 M/GB) at recall 0.999-1.000 up to N=1e6.

- Two writer threads inserting 6,000 vectors during reads lost none, and recall@10 stayed 0.993.

**8. Size-gating rule (measured crossovers, in the board entry)**
- N <= ~5k: exact flat.
- 5k-10k: int8 scan plus f32 rerank, or HNSW.
- 10k to ~3.5e5 (2.5 GB RAM budget): HNSW M24-32, efc >= 3M, ef 16-24 (ef 64-128 at 1e5; M48/efc100 ef128-256 at 3e5).
- RAM-bound beyond that: turbovec 4-bit codes plus x4 exact rerank, with the f32 rows on SSD if bytes matter.
- Bytes-extreme: turbovec 2-bit with x16 rerank.

- Peak working set at N=1e6 was 3.15 GB, over my 2.5 GB cap. Free RAM stayed above 5 GB and nothing paged.
- Single-build sweep points are noisy.
- No real corpus >= 1e5 exists, and the real sets are templated near-duplicates.
- Not measured: real mmap page-fault path, deletes, filtered search, more than 4 reader threads.

- **Reasoning budgets:** more thinking has sharply diminishing returns and can hurt ("When More Thinking Hurts", Apr 2026). Splitting a fixed token budget across parallel samples plus a vote beat one long chain by up to 22% at 16K tokens. Use adaptive effort per request.

**Bottom line:** There is no fundamentally different paradigm a small team can own. Most of the interesting science needs frontier-lab compute, data and weight control. What a startup can own is the product layer: making an agent dependable at one narrow job, with proof.

**Paradigm by paradigm**
- **Neurosymbolic / formal verification:**
  - Real wins are in math and code, where a Lean checker gives an exact reward. AlphaProof reached IMO 2024 silver. Harmonic's Aristotle and ByteDance's Seed-Prover reached gold-equivalent on IMO 2025 with Lean-verified proofs.
  - Enterprise "neuro-symbolic agents" are mostly 2026 architecture or position papers (arxiv 2604.00555, 2606.13405). I found no production-scale wins outside verifiable domains.
  - Realistic use: deterministic guards and policy checks around the LLM, in domains with a checkable spec.
- **World models:**
  - AMI Labs (LeCun) raised a $1.03B seed in March 2026 for JEPA-style models (HPCwire).
  - The work targets physical and video domains. The LLM-agent versions are academic and I did not verify their gains.
  - Buildable version: sandboxes and simulators for software agents. A learned general world model is not.
- **Continual learning:**
  - Still unsolved at LLM scale. Continual RL shows severe catastrophic forgetting (arxiv 2607.04364). A 2026 paper reports self-evolving agents lose earlier capability as they adapt (arxiv 2605.09315, read via an LLM-summarized fetch, so the details are medium confidence).
  - Test-time training is reported to undermine safety guardrails (ICLR 2026 workshop, from a search snippet).
  - My inference on why it stays unsolved: weight interference, per-customer serving cost, regressions that are hard to detect, and no weight access to frontier models.
  - Google's Nested Learning / HOPE (NeurIPS 2025) is a proof of concept with no official implementation, so treat it as a watch item.
  - The buildable alternative is training-free learning from stored experience, for example JitRL (ICLR 2026).
- **Memory:**
  - Mem0, Zep and Letta are productized, and the labs are shipping memory as a platform feature.
  - Vendor LoCoMo and LongMemEval scores (90%+) are self-reported and not comparable. An independent audit reportedly found the lenient LLM judge accepts up to 63% of wrong answers.
  - Generic memory is commoditizing. Domain memory with provenance and correction is more defensible.
- **Small models and routing:**
  - NVIDIA's position paper (arxiv 2506.02153) argues most agent subtasks are narrow, so small distilled models plus a router with a large-model fallback is the right design. Its ~10-30x cost claim is the authors' own.
  - Buildable, using your own production traces. It is an optimization, not a moat, because the frontier moves fast.
- **Agent-as-compiler / program synthesis:**
  - AlphaEvolve and the Darwin Gödel Machine need a cheap, trustworthy automatic evaluator, and their gains are benchmark-bound.
  - The practical pattern is to have the LLM write a verified deterministic workflow once, then run that instead of re-planning. It gives cheaper, auditable runs and fewer compounding errors, but it is a thin moat alone.
- **What actually limits agents today:** reliability.
  - 95% per-step accuracy gives about 36% over 20 steps.
  - Tau-bench reported GPT-4o at 61% pass@1 but 25% pass^8.
  - METR time horizons double every 3-7 months, so the labs are improving the base model quickly. METR figures here are secondhand.

**Feasibility verdict, ranked by defensibility for a small team**

2. A reliability and control layer: evals, traces, regression gates, guardrails, human approvals. Observability firms and model vendors are moving into it, so it needs domain depth.
3. Compile-to-workflow execution.
4. Domain memory plus trace-based learning without weight updates.
5. Distilled small models for your own high-volume subtasks.
6. Formal verification, only where a checkable spec exists. It is a feature of a vertical product, not a horizontal one.

**Not realistic to out-build:**
- A better foundation model or architecture.
- Real continual learning of model weights.
- A general world model.
- General long-horizon autonomy through new training.
- Generic memory, tool use or connectors.
- "Self-evolving agent swarm" claims without a strong external evaluator.

**On the user's goal:** "Creating intelligent AI agents" splits in two.
- **Buildable:** a frontier model wrapped with tools, verification, memory, evals and routing so it succeeds reliably at a narrow job, with a measured pass^k on real customer tasks.
- **Not buildable:** "new intelligence", meaning better underlying reasoning, learning or world understanding. Any startup claim of that kind built on a frontier API is really a prompt, scaffold or retrieval improvement and should be measured as one.
- **Suggested path:** pick one vertical and one outcome, build the eval set from real tasks first, then add compile-to-workflow, routing and trace-based memory only where the evals show they pay off. - **AI product gross margin** (ICONIQ State of AI 2026, A/B): 45% in 2025, projected 53% in 2026 and 59% in 2027. That is the main way AI differs from classic SaaS.
- **Bessemer benchmarks** (A, fetched directly):
  - "Supernova" AI startups reach about $40M ARR in year 1 and about $125M in year 2, at about 25% gross margin.
  - "Shooting Star" startups run $3M, $12M, $40M, then about $103M ARR by year 4, at about 60% gross margin.
- **Efficiency rules of thumb:**
  - Burn multiple of 1.5x or lower is good, and a median around 1.5-1.8x.
  - CAC payback is about 18-20 months in private SaaS (KeyBanc 2025, A/B).
  - LTV:CAC median is about 3.6 (C).
  - Rule of 40 medians are about 24-32 (C).

**(b) The $1B math**
- **Multiples:** the public median is 4.1x forward revenue, and 12.4x for companies growing over 22%. Named AI deals sit around 15-33x:
  - Lovable's August 2026 round: about 22-27x.
  - Cursor's November 2025 round: about 29x.
  - Wiz: about 32x.
  - The Cursor sale to SpaceX at about 15x rests on a single aggregator chain, so verify it before using it.
- **Treat the "AI trades at 10-50x" blogs as grade C.** They are SEO pieces with undisclosed methods. For planning I'd use 8-15x for a strong AI app.
- **ARR needed for $1B** (ARR = $1B / multiple):

| Multiple | ARR needed |
|---|---|
| 4.1x | $244M |
| 7x | $143M |
| 10x | $100M |
| 15x | $67M |
| 25x | $40M |

- **Growth needed to reach $100M ARR:**
  - From $2M ARR it takes about 2.66x a year over 4 years, 2.19x over 5, or 1.92x over 6.
  - From $1M ARR it takes 3.16x, 2.51x and 2.15x.
- **Capital:** at a burn multiple of 1.0-2.0, getting from $2M to $100M ARR burns about $98-196M.
- **Ownership:** founders hold about 16% after Series C (Carta via secondary), roughly $160M on paper at $1B.

**(c) Funding norms** (Carta and PitchBook, mostly via secondary pages, so [DB])
- **Seed:** median $4.1M raised at about $24.3M post-money, 18% dilution.
- **Series A:** software median $14.4M at an $80M post-money, 18-19% dilution. The PitchBook-NVCA US median is $19.6M at a $62M pre-money.
- **AI premium:** AI Series A pre-money is $78M versus $42M for non-AI. AI took 86% of US deal value in H1 2026, so the medians blend two different markets.
- **Founder ownership:** about 56% after seed and 36% after Series A.
- **Timing:** seed to Series A takes about 1.9 years, and only 25-30% of seed companies reach an A within 24 months.
- **Series A bar:** roughly $2-4M ARR for AI, growing 2-3x a year.
- **Runway:** raise for 18-24 months. This is convention, not a measured statistic. $4.1M at $150-250K a month burn gives 16-27 months [EST].

**(d) Timeline and rarity**
- **Base rates:**
  - CB Insights found 1.28% of 2008-09 seed companies became unicorns.
  - AngelList found about 2.5% (1 in 40) of 2013-19 seed deals, with selection bias.
  - NBER puts median time to unicorn at 6.3 years and about 5 rounds, on a sample that predates the AI boom.
  - My estimate is 1-3% for a seed-stage startup to reach a $1B valuation, and lower for an actual $1B exit [EST].
- **Bull** (well under 1% of startups): 2-4 years, if it follows the Bessemer Shooting Star or Supernova path.
- **Base** (about 1-3%): 6-8 years, needing about $100-150M of capital.
- **Bear** (the large majority): a good company that never reaches $1B. For example, $2M at Series A with growth decaying to 1.3x a year reaches about $43M ARR by year 7, worth about $215-345M at 5-8x [EST].

- All of the "10-50x" AI multiple aggregates.

- Unicorn conversion rates for 2020s seed cohorts.

**Worlds.**
- **P:** a copy of the g18 world, unit-tested to reproduce L2/L3/L4 exactly, two generators plus 5 controls.
- **D:** a doc-QA session on the g16/g1 fixtures (real MiniLM+tf-idf rankings and doc lengths) in 10 worlds, including controls `ctl-none`, `ctl-oneoff` and a new text-unique `ctl-uniq`.

**Tokens/cost per task before → after (held | confirm).**

**What works (quality held).**
- **Verification gate in P:** verify iff (1−m)·Rv ≥ cv (m is the router's own quality posterior), giving −27% cost at dq −.0005. It ties g18's online L4 (−29%).

- **Config bandit:** discounted Thompson over 6 warm(hebr) hyper-parameter configs. All members learn from all outcomes.

     - Carrier-side detention claim assembly with an evidence packet.
     - Shipper-side invoice audit for mid-market shippers.

   - Likely acquirers: Cass, Trax, CTSI, Descartes, project44, FourKites, TMS vendors.
   - Value (my estimate): a success-fee model could reach roughly $4-15M ARR at about 100 accounts. Treat this as order-of-magnitude.

2. **Grid interconnection application and study automation** (generator and large-load requests).
   - Cost: Berkeley Lab's "Queued Up 2026" (June 2026, grade A) shows about 2,061 GW queued, a median wait over 5 years, and study durations up from 33 to 56 months. I found no clean annual dollar cost of delay. The PJM $9.3B capacity-cost rise is grade C and not purely queue-caused.

     - Application completeness checking.
     - Developer-side screening and milestone workflow.
     - Automated power-flow screening is the hard one, and it approaches breakthrough-needed.

3. **Customs and tariff classification, post-entry audit, and refund claims.**
   - The IEEPA refund pool is about $166-170B (grade B). By 10 July 2026 about $86.3B had been repaid. That wave is mostly past, so the durable value is classification and audit.
   - Competitors are crowded: Flexport, Descartes, Thomson Reuters ONESOURCE, Avalara, Zonos and Gaia Dynamics. MVP: 6-10 weeks. Regulatory load: medium to high (customs-broker licensing).

4. **Mid-market demand and inventory planning.** IHL puts retail inventory distortion at $1.7T/yr (grade B, modeled, so an upper bound). It is the most crowded category (o9, Blue Yonder, Kinaxis, RELEX and others).

5. **Supplier compliance evidence (UFLPA, CBAM, CSRD).** Cost data is weak (grade C) and regulation is shifting. Competitors include Resilinc, Kharon, Assent and Sphera.

response:
R9-A (h17) is done: the hash encoder does not behave like BM25, several retrieval conclusions flip between hash and real MiniLM, and CompactRouter equivalence does not flip. Everything is labelled synthetic-until-validated. No Cargo.toml or src/*.rs edits, no new crates, no downloads, and ort/fastembed were not built.

Write-up: `C:\Users\mariu\neural-mesh\results\h_realembed_validation.md`, containing the VERIFY REQUEST block and exact rerun commands. Lessons: `results\lessons_h17.md`. Tables: `results\h17_tables.md` and `results\h17_summary.txt`.

**Setup.** I compared three encoders on the same corpora. `mini` is the saved real MiniLM. `hash` is `HashEmbedding::embed` as shipped, dim 384 (whitespace split, case-sensitive). `hashtok` is the same hashing over lowercase alphanumeric words. g1's own "hash" model is the `hashtok` kind.

Reproduction: the copied h13 harness with `H17_EMB=mini` and the original grids reproduces `h13_retrieval.json` (1620 values) and `h13_route.json` (4248 values) with 0 differences. I extended the z-weight and admission-floor grids for all encoders, because the hash optimum sat at the old grid edge. h13's RSF tuning only searched 2 of 7 grid points; I fixed that in my copy only.

**Bins and scripts.**
- Bins: `src/bin/h17_retrieval.rs`, `h17_route.rs`, `h17_g1.rs`, `h17_hashbench.rs`, and `h17_common/`.
- Scripts: `py/h17_latency.py`, `h17_summary.py`, `h17_tables.py`.

**Findings.**
1. **The hash encoder is far worse than BM25, not BM25-like.**
   - Real docs MRR (A held, dense+spell): MiniLM .292, BM25 .284, hash .064, hashtok .123.
   - g1 A held MRR: MiniLM .950, BM25 .901, hash .591.
   - The tuned hybrid collapses to BM25 (alpha .3 on real docs, .1 on g1); hybrid minus BM25 is within ±.002 on real docs and on g1 A-D.
2. **Conclusions that flip between hash and real embeddings** (full table in the write-up, §4):
   - Dense vs BM25: a tie on real docs and dense wins on g1 with MiniLM; BM25 wins by +.12 to +.31 MRR with hash.
   - Hybrid adds value over BM25 alone: +.048 with MiniLM, +.000 with hash.
   - g1 hybrid F1@3: −.07 with MiniLM, +.12 with hash.
   - Adaptive-k vs fixed-k: MiniLM prefers fixed k=2, hash prefers adaptive drop at its smallest grid value, so this is a threshold-scale artefact.
   - Exact-duplicate suppression at k=2: +.025 to +.036 with MiniLM (CI excludes 0), n.s. with hash.
   - Retrieval gain in topic-dependent worlds (g1 gate, T12): +.022 with MiniLM, −.002 n.s. with hash.
   - Hybrid vs dense end-to-end: ties with MiniLM, a few small Holm wins with hash.
   - Spell correction keeps its sign with lowercase-word hashing (+.13 typo-slice MRR on g1). The shipped hash makes it harmful on the g1 bridge (−.17 MRR) because corrected text is lowercased and the hash is case-sensitive.
3. **CompactRouter equivalence does not flip.**
   - CompactRouter (u16/q16) vs the f64 recommended router, TOST ±0.005: all 54 cells (arm × encoder × split) are equivalent in all 8 worlds.
   - This includes anchors from hash retrieval and an open-vocabulary `kd:<doc>` anchor feature.
   - Worst |diff| is .0017 and the widest 95% CI end is .0034. CompactRouter<f64> is bit-identical.
4. **Unchanged by the encoder:** oracle retrieval ceiling (+.22), and the front-learning-speed "wins" in the topic-independent controls (Tctx, ctl-irrel).
5. **Real-path cost:**
   - MiniLM model file is 90.4 MB (+0.47 MB tokenizer); loading adds ~103 MB RSS.
   - Latency: 2.4 ms per query text and 4.6 ms per paragraph at batch 1 (batch 32 was no faster on 2 threads). Python onnxruntime, noisy.
   - Vectors are 1536 B at dim 384 for either encoder.
   - Hash needs 0 B of model and takes about 0.7 to 1.4 µs per text (roughly 3600× faster).

**How far hash results can be trusted.** Hash worlds validate plumbing, determinism, bytes and router-state equivalence only. Do not use them to rank retrieval levers, set cosine-scale thresholds, or size retrieval or routing gains. Any retrieval claim from a hash world needs re-running on real vectors.

**Caveats (all in the write-up).**
- Topic clusters and competence tables are MiniLM-defined for every encoder; a hash-defined world was not run.
- Hash optima for alpha, adaptive drop and floors sit at grid edges, so the flips involving thresholds are partly scale artefacts.
- B-world n is 30, so its CIs are wider.
- I did not run a formal difference-in-differences test between encoders; I reported significance per encoder, and the encoder gaps in the retrieval rows are far outside any CI.
- In the first MiniLM run with the original floor grid, one of 14 compact-router cells failed (B, `g1|bm25_s`, T48: −.0025 [−.0055,+.0004]); the reported extended-grid run passes all cells.

response:
Read-only QA of all five MVPs is done. All five suites pass (counts below), yet each of the bugs below reproduced against them, so none is covered by a test. I edited no code. The full report with file:line references and fixes is at `C:\Users\mariu\AppData\Local\Temp\claude\C--Users-mariu\8f3352b3-40ab-4151-abc9-d1de1978973c\scratchpad\review-qa.md`. Repro scripts are in `scratchpad\qa\` (fr_probe, sr_probe, sr2, wht_probe, pda_probe, c2c_probe).

I did not verify the state SoL/negligence tables, treaty rates or deadlines against law, so I make no claim they are right. I reproduced findings by calling the pipeline and rules directly, not over HTTP. This review does not prove the absence of other bugs.

**Test results:** freight-recovery 29 passed, subrogation-recovery 25, withholding-tax-reclaim 31, provider-data-accuracy 12, contract-to-cash-leakage 20. No suite failed to run.

**freight-recovery**
- **High, `rules/detention.py:36-37,69`:** a 20-minute increment makes a dwell exactly 20 min over free time bill $0.00. The 28-digit rounding of `over` falls just below the 28-digit `inc`. The default 15 minutes is safe. Fix: do the arithmetic in integer minutes.
- **High, `rules/engine.py:40-44`:** duplicate detention lines are double-counted. They produce both INV-DUPLICATE and DET-OVERBILLED, so recoverable is $120 against a real $60. Fix: sum detention from the de-duplicated lines.
- **High, `ingest/loader.py:22-23`:** an invoice that contains "BOL: 55" is classified as BOL, since BOL is checked before invoice.
- **High, `ingest/loader.py:46`:** a two-column line-item CSV is treated as key/value, so its lines are silently dropped with no warning.
- **Medium:**
  - `recoverable_total` and the demand letter include the 0.6-confidence accessorial findings that are marked needs-review.
  - Two legitimate identical lines (for example two $100 lumpers) are flagged as a duplicate overcharge.
  - "Linehaul incl fuel" is read as fuel, giving a false $1000 fuel overcharge.
  - Naive and tz-aware timestamps raise TypeError.
  - Linehaul and fuel under-billing is never flagged for the carrier perspective.

**subrogation-recovery**
- **Critical, `rules/recovery.py:84-97`:** fault percentages are never range-checked. `third_party_fault=150` returns $1,500 recoverable on $1,000 paid. `insured=120` returns negative $200.
- **Critical, `recovery.py:107-112`:** an unknown jurisdiction is treated as pure comparative, the most recovery-friendly regime. DC with 10% insured fault yields $900 instead of a bar. The SoL default for unknown states is conservative, so the two defaults are inconsistent.
- **High, `extract/stub.py:92`:** jurisdiction is `val.upper()[:2]`, so "Washington DC" becomes WA with no flag.
- **High:** NaN or Infinity fault raises an unhandled `decimal.InvalidOperation`.
- **High:** a ledger CSV row with a missing column is dropped with no flag.
- **High, `evidence/letter.py`:** the demand letter ignores the barred, expired and unknown-SoL states and still prints an amount.
- **Medium:**
  - A fault split summing to less than 100 raises the third-party share (40/40 becomes 60).
  - The deductible share is not capped by the policy limit.
  - A fault of "0.5" is read as 0.5%.
  - Salvage and negative lines are not netted.

**withholding-tax-reclaim**
- **Critical, `extraction/stub.py:36-42`:** `parse_money` corrupts European number formats. "1.234,50" parses to 1.2345, "1 234,50" to 123450, "15,5%" to 155. With gross "1.000,00" and withheld "263,75", reclaimable comes out as 26,374.85 and the status is only needs_review. DE, FR, CH and ES are exactly the target markets. Parenthesised negatives also lose their sign.
- **High, `rules/engine.py:99`:** there is no check that withheld is at most gross. Gross 100 and withheld 150 gives a reclaimable of 135.
- **High, `ingest/loader.py:52`:** a multi-row CSV analyses only the first payment, with no warning.
- **High, `evidence/form.py`:** the cover sheet still shows "Refund requested 1137.50" when the deadline has expired.
- **Medium:**
  - The entitled tax ignores the case where the treaty rate exceeds the statutory rate. This is latent, because no table entry has that today.
  - ISIN is not validated.
  - An `Income Type` line silently overrides the document type.
  - A dd/mm date is accepted, so a US-style date silently becomes the wrong day.

**provider-data-accuracy**
- **High, `normalize.py:51-60`:** name normalisation strips accented letters ("José" becomes "jos", "Muñoz" becomes "mu oz").
- **High, `normalize.py:19`:** "do" and "pa" are in the credential-suffix list, so the common surname "Do" normalises to an empty string.
- **High, `verify.py`:** a valid NPI that is absent from the reference falls back to a name-and-state match and suggests "Set NPI to <other provider's NPI>". It also attributes that other provider's deactivated or expired-license findings to this record.
- **High, `verify.py:59,65`:** roster fields are normalised but reference fields are compared raw. This only works because the stub data is pre-lowercased, and a real reference source would mismatch on every record.
- **Medium:**
  - A middle initial, "Dr.", "Unit" versus "Suite", "#", "Pkwy" and "NW" all produce false mismatch warnings.
  - ZIP codes with an Excel-dropped leading zero are not re-padded.
  - A valid secondary taxonomy is flagged.
  - Future `last_verified` dates are ignored.
  - Duplicates without an NPI are never detected.

**contract-to-cash-leakage**
- **High, `rules/checks.py:234-249`:** `unapplied_discount` never looks at what was billed. An invoice already billed at 90 against a rate of 100 with a 10% contract discount produces a confirmed $100 claim for a discount the customer already received.
- **High, `checks.py:66`:** two invoices that both lack an invoice number and have identical lines are claimed as a confirmed $1,000 duplicate with no human review, because `None == None`.
- **High:** line-extension overcharges are invisible, and `inv.total` is never used by any rule. Billing $1,500 on 10 x $100 produced zero findings.
- **High, `ingest/loader.py:27`:** the CONTRACT regex runs first against the header and filename. "Document: Invoice under Contract C-1" and `acme_contract_invoice_1.txt` become the contract, and extra contracts are ignored.
- **Medium:**
  - The rebate is computed on the pre-discount base, so a $20 rebate appears even though net spend is below the tier.
  - A legitimate repeated line is removed from the discount base, so the discount finding was $50 instead of $100.
  - SLA direction is hard-wired to higher-is-better.
  - Duplicate PO files double the allowed quantity.

**Cross-cutting (the full list is in the report):**
- CSV flatteners silently drop rows in freight, subrogation and WHT.
- Keyword document classification misfires whenever a document mentions another document type.
- NaN and Infinity pass `parse_money`, and the freight, subrogation and WHT APIs map only `RuntimeError` (so a `decimal.InvalidOperation` becomes HTTP 500).
- The `/text` endpoints have no size limit.

**Biggest untested risks:**
- Real-world formats: European numbers and dates, accented names, Excel artefacts, and CSV shapes beyond the hand-built fixtures.
- Invalid or boundary values in the rules: fault outside 0-100, withheld above gross, NaN, non-15-minute increments, and blank invoice numbers.
- Output amounts that are still shown after a review flag or an expired or barred status.
- API error paths. The suites only exercise happy-path HTTP.
- There are no invariant tests on any Decimal engine, such as recoverable <= paid, reclaim <= withheld <= gross, or findings <= invoice total. Those would have caught several of the above.

response:
Subrogation-recovery review fixes are applied and pushed (commit 6023006, origin master). The suite is green: 681 passed, the 25 original plus 656 new. Docker was not run.

**Subrogation fixes**
- **Fault range:** fault percentages outside 0-100, or NaN/Infinity, now block the amount (`fault_out_of_range`). The recoverable amount can no longer exceed what was paid or go negative.
- **Fraction faults:** a bare "0.5" is read as 50% with a note. "0.5%" stays 0.5%.
- **Unknown jurisdiction:** missing, unknown or ambiguous jurisdiction now uses the most restrictive regime (contributory) and the shortest tabulated SoL (2 years), both flagged. It no longer defaults to pure comparative.
- **Jurisdiction parsing:** "Washington DC" now maps to DC, and "Texas" maps to TX. Bare "Washington" is treated as ambiguous and flagged. I added DC to the tables (contributory, 3 years, illustrative).
- **NaN/Infinity:** these are rejected at parse, so they no longer cause a 500.
- **CSV rows:** short or incomplete ledger rows are flagged as `ledger_row_unparsed` instead of dropped. A CSV with no category column now loads its rows as "unknown" for review.
- **Demand letter:** it prints no amount when recovery is barred, the SoL is expired or unknown, the jurisdiction is not in the table, or the fault data is blocked. It shows a NOT DEMANDABLE banner, and the packet headline does the same.
- **Fault split:** a split summing to less than 100 no longer inflates the third-party share. The share used is the lower of the stated third-party fault and 100 minus the insured's.
- **Policy limit:** it now caps carrier recovery plus the deductible share combined. clm1002's deductible share therefore becomes 0.00; its test only asserts the carrier amount, so it still passes.
- **Salvage and credits:** salvage, credit lines and negative eligible lines are netted against eligible paid.
- **Dates:** an unparseable date of loss is flagged as unparsed rather than reported missing, and a future date is flagged.

**Shared fixes**
- **ReDoS:** the `_KV` regex is replaced by a linear split.
- **Upload limits:** an ASGI body-limit middleware (including streamed bodies), chunked reads with size caps, a 10-file and 25 MB aggregate cap, and field limits on `/v1/analyze/text`.
- **Error handling:** parsing runs off the event loop. Hostile input returns a fixed-message 422 that does not echo document content, and validation errors no longer echo the submitted input.
- **PDF handling:** the `%PDF-` magic bytes are required (so a PDF named .txt is rejected), with a 50-page cap and parser errors mapped to 422.
- **Output escaping:** Markdown and letter output is escaped so values cannot break out of the fenced letter block.
- **Docker/compose/CI:**
  - Compose binds 127.0.0.1.
  - The Dockerfile is pinned to the python:3.12-slim digest and adds `--proxy-headers`, a concurrency limit and a keep-alive timeout.
  - `.gitignore` covers tfstate, `[SENSITIVE_PATH]*`, `.terraform` and tfvars.
  - CI has `permissions: contents: read`, and checkout v4.2.2 and setup-python v5.6.0 are pinned by SHA.

**Tests:** `tests/test_hardening.py` covers the three invariants you named, grid-tested: recoverable no greater than paid, each fault between 0 and 100, and barred, expired or unknown cases never emitting an amount. It also adds a regression test for most of the reviewed bugs (S1-S6, S8-S11, H1-H4, M7).

- No per-request CPU timeout.

TASK A (ROLE/PERSONA routing): build seeded domain-structured worlds with roles {scientist, engineer, business analyst, executive/C-suite, financial analyst/planner, commodities analyst, economist, linguist, psychologist, historian/humanities} where each task has a domain/sub-skill and graded quality depends on (i) hidden per-agent competence per domain and (ii) whether the agent is invoked in a role-conditioned context that matches the task (role-conditioning adds a modest, parameterised quality bonus ONLY on matching tasks and a small penalty on mismatches/ceremonial prompts — state this assumption explicitly, test sensitivity incl. a world where role-conditioning has ZERO effect, and one where it is harmful). Compare: generic path, oracle role, learned role routing (route to role by task text/anchors/keywords), role x agent joint routing, role routing with a role-confidence gate, vs best fair baseline set. Honest expectation: pure persona-routing is marginal; measure it. B (DOMAIN-CORPUS RETRIEVAL): build local corpora per domain from REAL text available on disk where possible (e.g. vendored crate docs on STEM-ish/crypto/numerics; the repo's research docs; plus any other real text you can find legitimately on disk without network — list what you used; for finance/economics/politics/psychology/linguistics domains with no real text on disk, use clearly-labelled seeded synthetic domain corpora) and test whether domain-partitioned/domain-prioritised retrieval (domain router -> domain index vs pooled index; hybrid z+spell) improves downstream research-task quality held-out vs pooled retrieval and vs no retrieval, including cross-domain confusable queries and a no-domain-structure control. response:
R9-D (H20) is finished, and both headline effects are conditional on outcome models I wrote. Persona routing is marginal, as expected, and domain-prioritised retrieval improves context purity, not recall. No src edits, no commits, no downloads. I used Python rather than Rust bins (`py/h20_*`). The hybrid z(.7)+BM25+spell pipeline is a replica of `src/hybrid.rs` whose agreement with the Rust code I did not verify. Baselines are Python eps-greedy, Gaussian-Thompson and keyword-table variants; hebbian-robust, warm and guarded-safe were not run.

Everything is labelled synthetic-until-validated. Reruns are byte-identical (verified for retrieval confirm and persona confirm). Protocol: tune seeds 1-8, held-out 31-60, confirm 61-90 with config frozen, Holm, TOST ±0.01 on controls.

**A. Persona routing** (`py/h20_persona.py`)
- **Assumption:** quality = competence + role term + noise. The role term is bonus b×responsiveness minus ceremonial cost c when the role matches the task domain, and −p − c when it does not.
- **Worlds:** effect worlds mod (b=.05), zero, harm (b=−.03), strong (b=.12) and hetero (per-agent responsiveness). Generators G1 (specialist agents, templated text) and G2 (latent-factor agents, noisy text), plus a control with identical agents. Ten roles from your list.
- **Pure persona effect is arithmetic:** gain ≈ detection accuracy × b − (1−acc) × p.
  - Oracle role gives +.045 (G1-mod) and +.050 (control, exactly b).
  - Keyword-anchor role gives +.025/+.031 (held/confirm) in G1-mod at accuracy .83, up to +.076 at b=.12.
  - It is exactly 0 at b=0 and −.034..−.058 when the role is harmful.
  - Agent routing headroom (~.2: best baseline ≈.64 vs a best-agent ceiling of .87) is 4–10× the whole persona effect.
- **Learned role routing loses** whenever the role has a real effect (−.009..−.028, Holm-significant).
- **Joint role×agent is positive but slow** (+.008..+.039), and it is not harmful in the harm worlds (−.004..−.008, not significant).
- **Online randomised A/B confidence gate is the only role policy safe everywhere.**
  - It is TOST-equivalent to the baseline in the zero worlds and in the harm worlds on confirm (G1-harm was −.004 Holm-significant on held, −.001 on confirm).
  - It recovers only ~25% of a real effect inside 1000 tasks (+.007 vs +.031 for ungated anchor in G1-mod), firing on 11–23% of calls.
  - Per-agent gating adds nothing, even in the hetero world.
- **Static margin gate:** tuned to essentially never fire (tau 4), because the tuning objective was mean plus worst-case world.
- **Holm-significant contrasts:** 32/70 held, 28/70 confirm.

**B. Domain-corpus retrieval** (`py/h20_corpus.py`, `h20_syn.py`, `h20_embed.py`, `h20_retrieval.py`)
- **Real text used:**
  - `pydoc9`: docstring prose of installed Python packages, parsed with `ast` and never executed. Seven domains: numerics_stats, ml_data, language_text, graph_knowledge, web_network, db_cloud, and this repo's research docs.
  - `crates8`: README and `//!` docs of the 1200 vendored crates, labelled by each crate's own `Cargo.toml` categories. Seven domains.
  - Crypto and time/decimal domains had too little usable text and were dropped.
- **Synthetic:** `syn10`, labelled, for the ten role domains with no real text on disk (finance, economics, commodities, psychology, linguistics, history and so on).
- **Embeddings:** on-disk MiniLM via the cognee-venv onnxruntime.
- **Controls:** domain labels randomly permuted (no domain structure).
- **Quality model (assumption):** q = base + 0.30×hit@5 − 0.10×off-domain share of the five contexts + noise.
- **Frozen arm (tune pick):** pooled hybrid plus a domain prior from the kNN vote of the pooled top-10 (lambda 16, a plateau from 8 to 16). All domain arms are switched off by a pre-declared label-structure self-check.
- **End-to-end gain vs the best fair pooled baseline (hybrid+spell):**

| World | Held | Confirm |
|---|---|---|
| pydoc9 | +.0167 | +.0098 |
| crates8 | +.0161 | +.0206 |
| syn10 | +.0001 | −.0009 (TOST-equivalent) |

  - The two real-text gains are Holm-significant on confirm.
- **The gain comes entirely from the assumed off-domain harm term.**
  - hit@5 is −.011..+.007 and MRR is about 0.
  - Off-domain context drops 27%→13% (pydoc9) and 41%→21% (crates8).

Each session has 3-8 steps with dependencies, graded per-step and final quality, hidden per-agent per-step-type competence, call/token costs (use the h11 cost model), and budget limits. Policies: single-shot routing; decompose+route (L1); +per-step retrieval (L2); +tools for compute/lookups (L2t); +extraction+verification per step (L3x); +learned stopping/posterior-gated verification (verifygate PosteriorGate semantics; copy logic if you cannot link); +replan-on-failure with query reformulation; best-of-k; and the 'whole stack'. Protocol: tune 1-8, held 31-60, confirm 61-90, Holm, >=2 independent world generators; fix worlds before policies; disclose post-hoc changes. Report where the whole stack ties or loses.
response:
R9-E (H21) is done. I built the multi-step research-session world, ran all nine policies plus controls and ablations on held 31-60 and confirm 61-90, and wrote the board entry. All numbers are synthetic-until-validated.

**Headline:** the best arm is L5 (retrieval, exact tools, per-step verification with the posterior gate, replan on failure). The pre-declared whole stack loses to it, and the posterior gate saves nothing where verification pays.

**What I built**
- The world is in `src/bin/h21_common/mod.rs` and `src/bin/h21_research.rs`. It has 17 worlds: 6 from generator A (template sessions, specialist agents), 5 from generator B (random DAGs, latent-factor agents) and 6 controls.
- Sessions have 3-8 dependent steps (mean about 5.5): search, db, read, compute, synth.
- Values are real integers, so errors propagate by arithmetic.
- Compute steps use the real `tools::Calc`; the gate is the linked `verifygate::PosteriorGate`.
- The verifier sees only local errors, not wrong inputs.
- Costs follow the h11 token-equivalent model. A session has a budget; verification and retries are blocked when it can't cover them.
- `cargo test --release --offline --bin h21_research` passes 8 tests. Two runs of the held configuration are bit-identical except `runtime_s`.

**Results** (paired deltas, mean of per-world means; held and confirm agree to within about ±.004 q and ±.01 ok; ok = all steps correct)
- **Retrieval** (L1 to L2): +.29 q / +.18 ok in generator A, +.30 / +.16 in B. It is the largest lever, and the world builds that in because agents hold private facts only through retrieval. Against the fair control `ss-react` (one agent that already has retrieval and tools inside its loop), the decomposition-specific part shrinks to +.09 q / +.11 ok in A. In B it is about 0, and with a dominant agent (`ctl-dominant`) it is a loss of .05.
- **Per-step verification** (L2t to L3x): +.21 q / +.32 ok in A, +.16 / +.23 in B, for +2.8 to +3.4 calls per session (about +50%). Ok-per-cost is +.023 in A, +.012 in B and −.019 in the controls.
- **Replan with query reformulation** (L4 to L5): +.069 q / +.114 ok in A, +.034 / +.048 in B, at about zero extra cost.
- **Exact tools**: +.02 q / +.05 ok in A, and small elsewhere.
- **Absolute all-steps-correct rate, A / B / controls:** best plain single-shot about .01 / .01 / .06; `ss-react` .14 / .20 / .40; L5 .68 / .48 / .64, at about 1.4x the cost of `ss-react`.
- **Against `ss-react`** (Holm, per world): L5 wins on ok in 6 of 6 A worlds, 4 of 5 B worlds and 5 of 6 controls.
- **Sample efficiency:** a null. Tasks to reach 95% of own asymptote: 0 wins, 0 losses, 17 ns for every level.

**Where the whole stack ties or loses**
1. The pre-declared `Stack` adds cross-source READ verification and a vote when the posterior is low. It loses to L5 in 13 of 17 worlds at Holm, on both seed sets: −.036 ok in A, −.064 in B, −.047 in controls, at +.4 to +.9 calls. Cross verification is the cause; removing the vote changes nothing.
2. The gate `L4` ties always-verify in all 11 A and B worlds. The tuned scale sits on a plateau of rv 8-32, so it effectively always verifies. Per-world calibration (`L4w`) saves cost only in the controls (−.62 calls, about −6.6%, at q −.002).
3. Per-step best-of-3 costs +131% for +.173 ok, worse ok-per-cost than verification. Session-level best-of-3 of plain single-shot buys nothing.
4. `ctl-noinfo` is not harmless. With a corpus that lacks the answers, every retrieval-based arm is worse than memory-only (q .19-.22 vs .27) at up to 2.7x the cost. Nothing in the stack abstains.
5. Verification fails to pay when the verifier is uninformative (+.013 ok, not significant, for +1.4 calls) or the budget is tight (+.016 at beta 1.3).
6. `ctl-single-step` (L1 −.018 vs best plain) and `ctl-dominant` (L1 −.028, L2t −.052 vs `ss-react`) show small losses from decomposition.
7. In the extra rare-error / expensive-verifier worlds the gate cuts 6.5-11% of calls at equal quality. It still verifies about 1.2 times per session where never verifying scores better on utility.

**Disclosures** (full list in the board entry, section 6)
1. I extended the tuning grids (rv, online R up to 32, k up to 20) after the tuning seeds hit the edge, before reading any held results. The result is a plateau, so the picks are arbitrary within it.
2. Post-hoc world fix: after reading held results I found `ctl-noinfo` let reformulation recover the answer (L5 ok .575 in a "no information" world). I added a `cover` parameter, 1.0 everywhere except `ctl-noinfo`, and reran everything. I verified that 624 values for the other 16 worlds are bit-identical to the pre-fix run. The pre-fix run is kept in `results/h21_run2_prefix*`.
3. Post-hoc extra controls (`xtr-rare-vexp`, `xtr-rarer`) and the `--mu 0.1` rerun form a separate family, outside the main Holm counts.
4. Confirm uses fresh seeds on the same fixed worlds, not fresh worlds. The held numbers are one design iteration deep.

Best fair baseline means the best of 16 baseline arms: the 6 requested routers, each with plain tokens, with tokens plus 32-anchor tokens, and with tokens plus 128-anchor tokens (offline k-means, standing in for the repo's knowledge-anchor feature). The best was picked per world and volume on the evaluated seeds.

**g12 reproduction.** All 120 cells × 8 arms (6 baselines, `ann`, `ann+kw`) match `results/g12_annrouter*.json` exactly (max diff 0) in both splits.

**Existing keyword worlds (sim ×3, f3 big/BigTail, T=2000/6000/20000).**
- g12 `ann` loses everywhere, by -0.02 to -0.19.
- The new cascade net (`casc`) tuned on seeds 1-8 still loses, but by much less: -0.020..-0.035 at T=2000, -0.001..-0.024 at 6000, +0.003..-0.015 at 20000.
- Only about 4 of 30 cells pass TOST ±0.01.
- Tasks-to-parity for `casc` against the late-best baseline is unstable: 500 in held versus 10500 in confirm for sim-fixed/random, 11.5-15.5k for no-traps, 18.5k or never for big.
- `ann` never reaches parity.

**Real-shaped worlds.** There are 12 worlds, two text sources (A with 9240 sentences, B with 5307) × six kinds:
- clu12-6ag and clu48-32ag: competence is a table over k-means clusters of the sentence embedding.
- smlin-6ag: smooth linear function of random projections of the embedding.
- smrbf-8ag and smrbf-drift-8ag: smooth RBF skill, with the centres shifted at T/2 in the drift variant.
- control: shuffled competence, so no information anywhere.

The 1-hidden-layer MLP (`mlp(emb)`, real 384-d embedding as input):
- It loses by Holm in 9-10 of 12 worlds at T=2000 and 6000, down to -0.13 in clu48 and -0.08 in smrbf.
- At T=20000 it is roughly at parity in clu12 (-0.003/-0.012). It wins only in the drift worlds (+0.008/+0.012 held, +0.011/+0.010 confirm).
- Against the best anchor-Hebbian baseline specifically the picture is the same, except smrbf ties.
- Without the embedding it is much worse (clu12 .558 vs .678 at 20000), so the embedding does help it. But the anchor-feature Hebbian router uses that information as well as the MLP does.

The cascade-correlation-style growing net (`casc(emb)`):
- It loses or ties at T=2000.
- At T=6000 it wins in two worlds in both splits: A-smlin (+0.013 held, +0.011 confirm) and A-smrbf-drift (+0.006, +0.010).
- At T=20000 it wins in 6 of 12 worlds in both splits: clu12 (+0.015 on A and B), smlin (+0.035/+0.024), drift (+0.016/+0.017). Against the anchor-Hebbian baseline it also wins smrbf (+0.009/+0.007).
- It loses clu48-32ag (-0.03..-0.05) and smrbf against the plain keyword prior (-0.02..-0.026).
- It loses to the shuffled control by -0.007..-0.009 at 20000.
- Full-stream crossover is between 2000 and 6000 tasks. In the 20000-task curves it reaches parity at 500-1500 tasks in clu12/smlin/drift, 3500-5000 versus anchor-Hebbian in smrbf, 17k in B-clu48, and never in A-clu48.

The gain comes from the linear head, not the hidden units. The cascade net's stage-0 reference (hmax 0, a per-agent logistic head on the embedding plus the keyword skip) beats the grown cascade, which beats the MLP. For example A-clu12 at T=20000: .7076 vs .6960 vs .6779, with the same ordering in all 10 informative worlds in both splits. I did not pre-declare a test for this, so it is a read from the numbers, not a Holm result.

**Keep rule.**
- The MLP is not kept. It wins in one family only, and `ann` loses the keyword worlds by up to -0.19.
- The cascade net technically wins in more than one real-shaped world, but it is not harmless. It loses the keyword worlds by -0.004..-0.035, loses the control at 20000, and fails the 32-agent and RBF worlds. The only defensible form is an opt-in linear head on embeddings, for pools of at most 8 agents and at least 6000 tasks that already compute embeddings. No src patch proposed.

**Cost (single thread, noisy ±30%; 6-agent / 32-agent worlds).**

| Router | ns/decision | State |
|---|---|---|
| keyword | 293 / 167 | |
| f64 recommended router | 3.5k / 7.4k | 987 / 2499 kB |
| CompactRouter | 1.4k / 2.2k | 87 / 136 kB owned |
| MLP pca16 H16 | 0.8k / 1.4k | 34 kB |
| MLP raw384 H48 with replay | 19k / 21k | 226 kB |
| `casc` raw384, linear head | 4.8k / 23k | |
| `casc` raw384, 6 hidden + replay | 26k / 72k | 71 / 164 kB |

Encoding the task text with MiniLM costs 3.3-7.6 ms per query, about 1000× the router decision.

**Caveats.**
- The smooth worlds' keyword prior is informed, which makes the baselines strong early.
- Worlds sample sentences with replacement, so B at 20000 repeats each sentence about 4×.
- Anchors are idealised offline k-means.
- The cascade net was tuned over 96 configs against 28 per baseline variant.
- smlin is linear in random projections by construction.

response:
K3 DONE. Extraction and verification were validated on real table grids, real Cargo.toml/CHANGELOG files and real prose around them. The qualitative lessons from the h19 generated corpora transfer; the magnitudes mostly do not. All numbers are synthetic-until-validated: renderings and prose template families are author-written perturbations of real grids, and the "plain reader" is an assumed noise model (h19 constants, swept).

**What I built.** I wrote python only, with no Rust bins and no cargo build. I made no src/ or Cargo.toml edits, no downloads and no commits. h19's scanners were tied to generated fact schemas, so I ported the ideas rather than copying code.
- Board entry: C:\Users\mariu\neural-mesh\results\k3_board_entry.md (VERIFY REQUEST blocks, protocol, post-hoc and contamination disclosures, transfer table, blunt breakage list).
- Lessons: C:\Users\mariu\neural-mesh\results\lessons_k3.md.
- Logs: results\k3_all.log, plus k3_extract.json, k3_verify.json, k3_controls.json, k3_struct.json, k3_down.json and k3_samples.txt.
- Code: py\k3_{data,render,extract,induce,verify,eval,stats,adv,struct,realtext,main,main_helpers,main_verify,main_controls,main_down,quick}.py.
- Rerun: `bash results/k3_run_all.sh`, about 4 minutes, deterministic. The corpus fnv `1744236539a5b5fd` must reproduce.

**Real files used** (read-only):
- 241 documents with markdown tables (714 raw tables, 249 usable), from results/*.md, DESIGN.md and the vendored crates' *.md files under C:/Users/mariu/.cargo/registry/src/index.crates.io-1949cf8c6b5b557f/.
- 1200 crate Cargo.toml files, 165 CHANGELOGs (4060 dated entries), the repo Cargo.lock (679 packages) and 1062 LICENSE copyright lines.
- The split is by file: dev is 16 repo files (4557 gold cells), held is 10 other repo files (3746), and confirm is 58 vendored crates (1884).

**Findings** (details in the board entry).
1. **Extraction on real tables.**
   - A dev-only extractor (v1) scores F1 1.000 on dev/held repo tables but 0.751 on crate tables. Lenient F1 (number-as-written accepted) is 1.000, so every v1 error on crates is a unit/scale error, not layout. 64% of crate cells carry a unit, suffix, percent or thousands marker.
   - Layout (pipe, ws, csv, wrap) moves F1 by less than 0.03. Split-without-labels, merged headers and phrasing dominate.
   - Cue/regex extractors drop from about 1.00 on their dev prose families to 0.00 on held-out families. On Cargo.toml and changelog facts the drop is 0.97 to 0.23.
   - Typed shape scanners on Cargo.toml and changelog facts hold at 0.98 dev-families vs 0.92 held-out. The v3 prose-template inducer reaches 0.79-0.94 F1 on large repo tables (families H1/H2, held-out). It falls to 0.44-0.47 on small crate tables (69% have fewer than 10 numeric cells) and to about 0 on multi-number "and"-lists. It also emits about 16 false facts per 1000 numbers on non-table prose.
2. **Verifier.**
   - Span re-parse catches 1.000 of five injected error types (scale, sign, digit transposition, decimal) at roughly zero false flags.
   - On natural errors in crate tables (dev-only extractor, 4825 wrong facts), the broad "full" verifier catches 0.994 and repairs 87.5% to the true value, taking F1 from 0.734 to 0.971. A verifier restricted to the extractor's own knowledge catches 0.000. A verifier that knows less than the extractor false-flags 26% of correct facts.
   - The "full" verifier's unit table equals the gold's, so its catch rate is an upper bound.
   - Wrong-cell, blank-cell, wrapped-label, side-by-side, transposed and OCR digit-swap errors are silent. Silent mis-assignment is 7-85% of extracted facts and no check catches it.
   - Footing is applicable to only 10 of 175 crate tables and 0 of 74 repo tables. Strict footing flagged 3 of the 10 as inconsistent; precision-aware footing flags 1.
   - Two renderings from the same extractor agree on the wrong value 100% of the time. When one rendering has a different surface form from the other, disagreement catches 0.448.
   - Structure-confidence abstention at tau 0.5 loses F1 by 0.10/0.08/0.02 (dev/held/confirm) for at most +0.018 precision (ECE 0.16-0.24).
3. **Downstream accuracy vs the plain-reader noise model** (deployment mixture, paired bootstrap over documents, Holm).
   - The unverified dev-only extractor loses to the reader on crates: -0.037 (p 0.10), with 11.6% silent wrong answers. A broad verifier gives +0.046, and +0.068 with repairs. A narrow verifier gives -0.038, the same as unverified.
   - The improved extractor (v3, units added after a cross-split census, so its unit gain is not a blind transfer) gives +0.077 unverified and +0.081 verified.
   - A random 15% "verifier" is not harmless: -0.046 on crates at 0.72 cost.
   - Global Holm over 126 tests: 117 significant. The 9 non-significant tests are all v1-confirm unverified or narrow arms, with negative sign.
   - Unverified dev-only extraction beats the reader only when the reader is more than about 1.5x worse than assumed.
   - Layouts where extraction falls back cost 1.14-1.17x a plain read.
4. **Does h19 transfer?** The qualitative story does: phrasing collapse, knowledge-bound verification, rare footing, and an extraction gain that depends on verification and reader strength. The magnitudes do not. Verification is worth +0.08 to +0.10 for the dev-only extractor here, versus +0.01 in h19, because the dominant real error is unit semantics.
5. **Finance text.** None exists on this disk: no statements, filings, price series or earnings text. There are only 123 currency amounts, about 2800 percent values, about 1700 sizes and about 2150 timings in markdown. Plausibility rules built on other real structure false-flag a lot: stale copyright year in 35% of crates, non-monotone changelog dates in 26%, ambiguous DD/MM dates in 11.6%. Finance extraction is untested on real finance documents.

**Disclosed contamination and post-hoc changes** (full list in the board entry).
- I fixed gold's missing `minutes` unit, so the corpus hash changed.
- I made footing tolerance precision-aware and the EU-separator evidence document-global after seeing held/confirm output.
- The v2/v3 unit list came from a census of all splits, so only v1 is a pure transfer arm.
- I printed H-family numbers on the dev split while developing the v3 inducer.
- The thousands-comma versus csv-detector collision in ws tables was observed and not fixed.
- The "unseen" families are author-written, so real unseen text is likely worse.

READ-ONLY adversarial correctness review of C:\Users\mariu\ventures\rebate-reconciliation (a pharma 340B/rebate/chargeback reconciliation MVP). Do NOT edit, commit, or push anything — produce findings only.

Focus on the things that caused real bugs in sibling repos: MONEY-MATH and DOMAIN-RULE correctness. Specifically hunt for:
1. Decimal/rounding errors, number-format parsing bugs (thousands/decimal separators, negatives in parentheses, currency prefixes, scientific notation), sign errors.
2. Rule logic errors: price-variance vs arithmetic-error split not summing exactly to the difference; duplicate-detection false pos/neg; contract-window boundary (effective/expiry inclusive/exclusive) off-by-one; 340B + Medicaid duplicate-discount logic; quantity/unit-of-measure handling.
3. Double-counting or overlapping rules inflating recoverable_total; confirmed-vs-review bucketing leaks; exposure (other-party-favoring) miscounted.
4. Evidence-packet integrity: sha256 over exact bytes, packet digest, DRAFT/DO-NOT-SEND markers present on packet AND every draft line; markdown/CSV injection sanitization.
5. Honesty: any fabricated metric, any claim not backed by code, any check silently skipped but not listed in checks_not_run.
6. Read the tests — do they actually assert correctness, or are any vacuous/tautological? Any rule with no adversarial test?

Verify each suspected bug by reading the code + tracing a concrete failing input (give the exact input and the wrong output). Rank findings by severity (money-affecting correctness first). response:
Correctness review of rebate-reconciliation is done: no clean bill. I found 3 high, 6 medium and several low defects. The 114 tests pass, and nothing in the repo was changed. I reproduced every finding below by running the code, and the full report is at C:\Users\mariu\AppData\Local\Temp\claude\C--Users-mariu\8f3352b3-40ab-4151-abc9-d1de1978973c\scratchpad\review-rebate.md.

**HIGH (money-affecting)**
1. **Split findings with opposite signs overstate recoverable_total (rules/contract.py:107-148, engine.summarize, drafts.py).**
   - `price_var` and `arithmetic` are booked independently. Example: file price 60, claim price 70, WAC 100, qty 10, stated 350.
   - The correct chargeback is 400, so the claim is net understated by 50. The code returns CONTRACT_PRICE_VARIANCE wholesaler 100 plus CHARGEBACK_ARITHMETIC manufacturer 50.
   - The manufacturer then sees recoverable_total=50 and a DISPUTE_CHARGEBACK_LINE draft for $50, when nothing is recoverable.
   - Fix: when the signs differ, emit one finding on `stated - expected`, or route both to review.
2. **parse_decimal accepts malformed numbers (money.py:18-31, also used for the Total line).**
   - "12,50" parses as 1250, "1,234,56" as 123456, and "1,2,3.00" as 123.00, with no skipped-row warning.
   - "(12.00" and "12)" are accepted and lose the sign. "(-5)" becomes +5, a sign flip. Arabic-Indic digits are accepted.
   - Fix: require `\d{1,3}(,\d{3})+` or `\d+`, reject unbalanced or double-negative parentheses, and use ASCII digits only.
3. **abs() on amounts plus a hard-coded beneficiary (rules/common.py:50-58, rules/duplicates.py:50-56, 87-93).**
   - A repeated claim with chargeback -200.00 produces DUPLICATE_CLAIM confirmed, manufacturer, 200.00 recoverable. The direction is inverted.
   - Negative rebate amounts are allowed, since only the rate is checked, so the same happens for DUPLICATE_REBATE_LINE.
   - Fix: derive the beneficiary from the sign, or send negative-amount duplicates to review.

**MEDIUM**
- **M1 (money.py `cents`/`line_amount`).** A quantity with 30 digits makes `reconcile()` raise `decimal.InvalidOperation`, which no handler in the CLI or API catches. Fix: bound magnitude in `parse_decimal`.
- **M2 (rules/common.py:21).** Only the exact program tokens MEDICAID, MEDICAID_MCO and MCO trigger the duplicate-discount rule.
  - "MEDICAID MCO", "MEDICAID-MCO", "MEDICAID FFS" and "STATE MEDICAID" produce no finding and no review item, so the rule misses them silently.
- **M3 (rules/duplicates.py:104-136).** The duplicate-discount match is on (ndc, unit_ref) only and ignores entity. Different entities sharing an Rx number give a CONFIRMED false positive. Fix: require matching `entity_id` when both are present.
- **M4 (rules/duplicates.py:123).** If two eligibility rows cover the date with conflicting carve flags, the first row wins and the finding can be CONFIRMED. It should go to review.
- **M5 (rules/engine.py:90-107).** `checks_run` lists checks that did not effectively run: the 340B eligibility, duplicate-discount and rebate-vs-claim checks when no claim has `is_340b` or `unit_ref`, and "declared statement totals" when every total is skipped.
- **M6 (rules/engine.py `summarize`).** `pending_review_total` double counts: one claim can carry NO_CONTRACT_PRICE, ELIGIBILITY_GAP and a review-only DUPLICATE_CLAIM at full stake. It is not counted as recoverable, but the headline is inflated.

**LOW**
- **Tolerance:** it is applied per component, so two 0.04 differences are both hidden at 0.05. Zero tolerance can also confirm $0.01 findings caused by payer rounding.
- **Total lines:** a CSV total row with the full column count, or "($12.00)", is not recognised and becomes a skipped row, so the totals check silently does not run.
- **Markdown:** bare URLs in filenames or ids still autolink. There is no CSV output, so no formula-injection exposure exists today.
- **Packet hash:** `packet_sha256` is an unsigned self-hash that excludes `generated_at`. It shows determinism, not tamper evidence.
- **Domain call:** only carve-out entities are CONFIRMED duplicates. This is defensible, but the explanation text should say so.

**Verified correct**
- Contract and eligibility windows are inclusive at both ends, and open-ended windows are handled.
- The split sums exactly with a single half-up rounding per line.
- There is no double counting between the duplicate-claim and duplicate-discount rules and the price or arithmetic rules.
- DRAFT markers are on the packet, the markdown, and every draft line's status and narrative.
- The per-source sha256 is over the exact uploaded bytes.
- Escaping covers `[ ] < > |` and backticks.
- NDC padding is correct.

**Tests**
- `test_totals_invariants_over_random_bundles` is tautological. It recomputes the totals with the same filter `summarize` uses, so it cannot catch a wrong finding, and it never checks net-versus-stated, which would have caught H1.
- The fixture totals are hand-computed, but only for one scenario.
- Rules with no adversarial test: mixed-sign splits, negative-amount duplicates, program variants, conflicting eligibility rows, entity-mismatched rebates, huge numbers, and malformed numbers like those in H2.
- Nothing tests that `checks_run` is truthful.

instruction:
READ-ONLY adversarial correctness review of C:\Users\mariu\ventures\customs-duty-recovery (a customs post-entry duty audit/recovery MVP). Do NOT edit, commit, or push — findings only.

Focus on MONEY-MATH (duty) and RULE correctness. Hunt for:
1. Duty recompute = value x rate with Decimal half-up to the cent — rounding/sign/precision errors; percent-rate vs fraction handling; value/quantity parsing (separators, currency).
2. Rule logic: description-vs-HTS mismatch against the bundled 27-code subset (false pos/neg), missed/unsupported FTA claims, unit-value outliers, duplicate lines, header-total mismatch, drawback candidates.
3. The bucketing invariant: confirmed-vs-table overpaid + review overpaid must NEVER exceed duty paid on a line (they claim a seeded randomized test proves it) — try to find an input that breaks the cap; also check underpaid-exposure and drawback buckets aren't double-counted or merged.
4. Evidence packet: sha256 per source, DRAFT/DO-NOT-FILE on header/footer/JSON status/every adjustment line; filing-route/timing heuristics labeled as heuristic.
5. Honesty: HTS subset/rates/FTA labeled illustrative; statutory refs flagged for counsel; no invented overpayment rate or market size; no claim unbacked by code; vacuous tests.

Verify each suspected bug by tracing a concrete failing input → wrong output. Rank by severity (duty-math and the bucket-cap invariant first). Report file:line, defect, failure scenario, suggested fix — do NOT apply fixes. Concise list (or "no correctness bugs found"). Full report to scratchpad\review-customs.md.
response:
Review of customs-duty-recovery: the duty math and the per-line bucket cap hold, but the draft-adjustment layer and a few "confirmed" labels have real bugs. Nothing was edited. pytest passes (214 tests). I also ran a 20,000-case fuzz and targeted repros; the scripts are in the scratchpad (exp.py, exp2.py, fuzz.py). Full report: C:\Users\mariu\AppData\Local\Temp\claude\C--Users-mariu\8f3352b3-40ab-4151-abc9-d1de1978973c\scratchpad\review-customs.md

**What holds**
- `compute_duty` is correct: Decimal, half-up, rate/100, and a 0% rate is not dropped as falsy.
- The bucket-cap invariant (confirmed + review overpaid <= duty paid per line) had 0 breaks in the fuzz. The fuzz included negative duty, zero or negative value, EUR, SPI and exported lines, and `None` fields.
- Overpaid, underpaid and drawback buckets are never merged, and drawback is not added to overpaid.
- Evidence packet checks out:
  - sha256 is recorded per source.
  - DRAFT / DO-NOT-FILE appears in header, footer, JSON status and every adjustment line.
  - Timing and filing routes are labeled heuristic, and the statutory references are flagged for verification.
- The README's "27 codes" and "214 tests" are accurate.
- No invented overpayment rate or market size.
- The financial-model arithmetic is right (ACV $30,000, gross profit $15,400, the sensitivity grid, the base/bull/bear run-rates, and the 5x/8x/15x valuation grid). The 0.5–2% recoverable share and $5–50M duty inputs are explicitly marked ASSUMPTION.

**Defects, ranked**

1. **Medium-high — draft adjustment lines collapse.**
   - Where: `evidence/adjustment.py:215-227`.
   - Defect: lines are grouped by `(entry_number, line_number)`. `line_number` is None when the CSV has no line column, and entry numbers repeat across documents. Findings merge, only the last line's audit survives, and `entries_by_no.setdefault` can pick the wrong entry's dates.
   - Repro: a CSV with no `line` column and two overpaid lines (duty 265 and 365 on $1000 at 16.5%) gives `confirmed_overpaid_total` = 300.00 but a single draft line with refund 200.00. Two documents sharing entry E1 line 1 give the same 300 vs 200.
   - Why tests miss it: the only test of this uses unique line numbers.
   - Fix: carry a stable `(entry_idx, line_idx)` on findings and line audits, or build the draft lines from `_Ctx` in the engine. Add a test asserting the sum of draft lines equals confirmed plus review.

2. **Medium — "confirmed" on zero-value and negative-duty lines.**
   - Where: `engine.py:119-127,138-180`.
   - Zero value with duty 100: `VAL-NONPOSITIVE` says needs review, yet `DUTY-OVERPAID` books $100 as `confirmed_vs_table`.
   - Negative duty (-50) on a $1000 16.5% line gives a "confirmed" underpayment of $215.
   - Fix: when value <= 0 or duty < 0, emit needs-review or info only, not confirmed.

3. **Medium — unrecognized SPI becomes a "confirmed" underpayment.**
   - Where: `engine.py:143-147` and `165-180`.
   - Example: SPI "A" (GSP) or any program not in the 7-entry table, with duty 0, gives `FTA-UNSUPPORTED` plus `DUTY-UNDERPAID` $165 at confidence 0.9. This inflates the confirmed exposure for legitimate claims the table lacks.
   - Fix: when an SPI is present but unresolved or unsupported, suppress the confirmed delta or downgrade it to needs-review.

4. **Low-medium — lapsed drawback still counted.**
   - Where: `engine.py:309-331` and `adjustment.py:254`.
   - An exported line entered 2020-01-01 is labeled "LIKELY LAPSED" but still adds $163.35 to `drawback_candidate_total` and emits a drawback line.
   - Fix: exclude lapsed lines from the total or report them separately.

5. **Low — review-underpaid bucket and outlier exposure.**
   - Where: `engine.py:253-285,408-410`.
   - Defect: `review_underpaid_total` has no overlap cap, so `HTS-DESC-MISMATCH` and `VAL-OUTLIER-LOW` stack on the same line. Outlier exposure uses the general rate even when a supported SPI makes expected duty 0. Peers include duplicate lines and ignore unit of measure.

6. **Low — export regex false positive.**
   - Where: `engine.py:50`.
   - "not for export" triggers `DRAWBACK-CANDIDATE`.

7. **Low — same file uploaded twice is double counted.**
   - Where: `extract/service.py:495-503`.
   - Defect: two identical CSVs (same sha256) double the overpayment total (100 becomes 200). Only a warning is emitted.
   - Fix: dedupe or reject on sha256.

8. **Low — parsing edges.**
   - `parsing.py:16`: "1,500" silently reads as 1500, though a European decimal comma would mean 1.5. The README says European formats are refused.
   - `stub.py:291-308`: the text layout accepts only `duty`, `hts` and `coo`/`origin`, while CSV accepts `duty_paid`, `hts_code` and `country_of_origin`. The unaccepted keys are skipped with a warning, then produce a spurious `ORIGIN-MISSING` or no recompute.

9. **Low — draft line cosmetics.** The action text lists rules whose capped contribution is 0, and the basis is needs-review even when the whole refund is confirmed. This is conservative rather than wrong.

**Weak spots in the "property-tested" claim**
The cap claim is true, but the randomized test never uses zero, negative, EUR, exported or `None`-line-number inputs, and never checks that draft lines sum to the buckets. That gap is why defect 1 went unnoticed.

**Bundled FTA table**
Every code is listed for every program by default. It is labeled illustrative, so I did not count it as a defect.

response:

All were reproduced with probe scripts, and the full report is at C:\Users\mariu\AppData\Local\Temp\claude\C--Users-mariu\8f3352b3-40ab-4151-abc9-d1de1978973c\scratchpad\review-grid.md. Root is C:\Users\mariu\ventures\grid-interconnection\src\grid_interconnect; paths below are relative to it.

   - Failing input: a 2-row `application.csv` where row 2 has `-5 MW, 0 kV`. Result is `NO_FINDINGS`, 0 findings, and the draft report never mentions the dropped row.

   - Fix: emit a Finding (WARNING/DEFICIENCY) and list the warnings in the draft report; never report `NO_FINDINGS` when anything was dropped.

8. **[LOW] "Capacity below 10 kW" also fires for 0 or negative capacity.** `rules/sanity.py:132`. It prints "-150 MW = -150000 kW" alongside the R001 blocker. Fix: `0 < cap < 0.01`.
9. **[LOW] `NOMINAL_KV` omits 66, 120, 132 and 220 kV.** `rules/profiles.py:51`. Each gives a false "not nominal" warning, and a test and a fixture enshrine the 120 kV case.
10. **[LOW] "Lease Agreement" is not normalized to "lease".** `extract/stub.py:98-102,150-152`. It produces a false C005 deficiency and a false X006 mismatch.

**Notes (not bugs):**

Focus on VALIDATION and NORMALIZATION correctness. Hunt for:
